claim: Both novels ask what a maker owes the being he makes. Victor's answer is a debt he cannot bear and runs from; Moreau's is that nothing is owed, so the made thing becomes material to be reworked and thrown away.

from.exact: These creatures you have seen are animals carven and wrought into new shapes.

to.exact: A new species would bless me as its creator and source

alignments.same: Each maker describes his work as bringing new kinds of being into existence.
alignments.differs: Victor imagines the new species thanking him as a father; Moreau calls his creatures carved animals and expects nothing back.

from.exact: To this day I have never troubled about the ethics of the matter

to.exact: breathless horror and disgust filled my heart

alignments.same: Each passage records the maker's feeling once the work stands in front of him.
alignments.differs: Victor's disgust arrives at the moment of success and makes him abandon the creature; Moreau feels nothing and keeps working.

question: Is Moreau's indifference a worse failure than Victor's flight, or a more honest version of it?

substitution.note: With The Birth-Mark in place of Frankenstein the claim fails: Aylmer does not make a new being and loves what he works on.

claim: Moreau is answering the vivisection debate of the 1890s rather than Frankenstein: pain, not parenthood, is its subject, and Wells's own essay on plasticity frames it as physiology.

from.exact: Each time I dip a living creature into the bath of burning pain

to.exact: I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body.

alignments.same: Both passages measure the maker's labour in years of method.
alignments.differs: Victor works on dead matter and never mentions pain; Moreau's method is pain inflicted on living animals.

question: Does the Frankenstein comparison hide what is specific to Moreau?

substitution.note: The claim depends on Frankenstein's dead matter versus Moreau's living animals; The Birth-Mark also operates on the living, so the contrast weakens but the claim about pain still separates them.

claim: Victor's science adds a being to the world and the being outlives his love; Aylmer's science subtracts a flaw from a beloved being and kills her at the moment of perfection. Both ask whether a scientist can improve on what nature made.

from.exact: has it never occurred to you that the mark upon your cheek might be removed?

to.exact: if I could bestow animation upon lifeless matter

alignments.same: Each project begins as a question about what science might do to a body.
alignments.differs: Victor wants to give life to the dead; Aylmer wants to take a mark away from the living.

from.exact: the parting breath of the now perfect woman passed into the atmosphere

to.exact: the beauty of the dream vanished

alignments.same: Each experiment ends the moment it succeeds.
alignments.differs: Victor's creature lives and Victor turns from it; Georgiana dies and Aylmer's ideal survives only as loss.

question: Which failure does each story blame: the science, or the scientist's idea of perfection?

substitution.note: With Moreau in place of The Birth-Mark the subtract/add contrast fails: Moreau reshapes animals rather than removing a flaw from a beloved.

claim: Both stories ask whether a maker can cure the loneliness he built into his creature by making it a mate. Victor, asked, tears the half-made female apart; Rappaccini, unasked, remakes a stranger into a bridegroom, and the daughter he calls gifted dies refusing the gift.

from.exact: thou art no longer lonely in the world

to.exact: You must create a female for me, with whom I can live in the interchange of those sympathies necessary for my being.

alignments.same: Each maker is asked to end a made being's solitude by making it a companion of its own kind.
alignments.differs: The Creature demands the mate and Victor destroys her unfinished; Beatrice never asked, and her father has already turned Giovanni into one without his consent.

from.exact: Wouldst thou, then, have preferred the condition of a weak woman, exposed to all evil and capable of none?

to.exact: A new species would bless me as its creator and source

alignments.same: Each maker expects the being he made to be grateful for what he gave it.
alignments.differs: Victor's hope dies the moment he sees his creature; Rappaccini still calls the poison a gift while his daughter is dying.

from.exact: I would fain have been loved, not feared

to.exact: I am malicious because I am miserable

alignments.same: The made being tells its maker that what he gave it shut it out from love.
alignments.differs: The Creature turns his exclusion into threats and murder; Beatrice blames no one but asks to be loved, and dies.

question: Is Rappaccini's unasked gift of a bridegroom a better answer to the Creature's demand than Victor's refusal, or a worse one?

substitution.note: With Moreau or The Birth-Mark in place of Frankenstein the claim fails: no made being asks for a mate, and no maker makes or refuses one.

claim: Hawthorne stages the same death twice and reverses its cause. Georgiana dies when science removes the mark that made her human; Beatrice dies when an antidote removes the poison that made her inhuman. Perfection kills one, the ordinary kills the other, and both drink what a man who loves them hands over.

from.exact: I will drink; but do thou await the result.

to.exact: I joyfully stake all upon your word

alignments.same: A woman takes the draught a man brings her, knowing it may kill her.
alignments.differs: Georgiana drinks out of faith in her husband's science; Beatrice drinks first so that Giovanni, who distrusts her, can watch what it does.

from.exact: as poison had been life, so the powerful antidote was death

to.exact: the parting breath of the now perfect woman passed into the atmosphere

alignments.same: The woman dies at the moment the trait that set her apart is taken away.
alignments.differs: Removing the mark makes Georgiana perfect; removing the poison makes Beatrice ordinary, and it is the ordinary that kills her.

from.exact: and is this the upshot of your experiment!

to.exact: Then a hoarse, chuckling laugh was heard again!

alignments.same: Each story ends with a voice that greets the death as a verdict on the experiment.
alignments.differs: Aminadab's laugh mocks Aylmer's science from below; Baglioni's cry blames Rappaccini, though his own antidote did the killing.

question: If taking away the mark and taking away the poison both kill, what was the flaw protecting?

substitution.note: With Frankenstein or Moreau in place of The Birth-Mark the claim fails: neither ends with a woman drinking a cure that removes what marked her.

claim: Both books turn on a maker's confession about the being he brought to life. Victor's creature is another body, which he abhors at first sight and abandons; Jekyll's is himself, which he welcomes in the mirror and keeps feeding. Shelley's maker is ruined by disowning what he made, Stevenson's by owning it.

from.exact: And yet when I looked upon that ugly idol in the glass, I was conscious of no repugnance, rather of a leap of welcome.

to.exact: the beauty of the dream vanished, and breathless horror and disgust filled my heart

alignments.same: Each maker recalls his first look at the ugly living thing his experiment produced.
alignments.differs: Victor runs from the sight in disgust; Jekyll, looking into a mirror, feels a leap of welcome and calls the ugly face his own.

from.exact: Jekyll had more than a father’s interest; Hyde had more than a son’s indifference.

to.exact: No father could claim the gratitude of his child so completely as I should deserve their’s.

alignments.same: Each maker thinks of himself as the father of what he makes.
alignments.differs: Victor expects a child's gratitude and deserts the creature he gets; Jekyll keeps a father's care, and it is Hyde who feels nothing for him.

from.exact: For two good reasons, I will not enter deeply into this scientific branch of my confession.

to.exact: you expect to be informed of the secret with which I am acquainted; that cannot be

alignments.same: In his confession each maker refuses to tell how the thing was done.
alignments.differs: Victor keeps the secret so that Walton cannot repeat his crime; Jekyll gives a moral reason, then the plainer one: his discoveries were incomplete.

question: Is Jekyll's welcome of Hyde a cure for Victor's disgust, or the same failure turned inside out?

substitution.note: With Moreau or Rappaccini's Daughter in place of Frankenstein the claim fails: neither maker recoils from his first sight of what he made, and neither tells his story as a confession. Dorian Gray in place of Jekyll fails too: Dorian did not make the portrait and leaves no confession.

claim: Wilde takes over Stevenson's gentleman whose sins are worn by a second shape, and turns it inside out. Jekyll must leave his body to sin as Hyde; Dorian sins in his own unchanging face while the portrait ages for him. Both end in a locked room the household breaks into, where the dead man wears the face of his sins.

from.exact: stand, with a mirror, in front of the portrait that Basil Hallward had painted of him

to.exact: And yet when I looked upon that ugly idol in the glass, I was conscious of no repugnance, rather of a leap of welcome.

alignments.same: Each man looks at the ugly face his sins have made and takes pleasure in it.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's glass shows Hyde's face as his own living body; Dorian needs a mirror to set his still fair face beside the ugly one on the canvas.

from.exact: felt keenly the terrible pleasure of a double life

to.exact: I was the first that could plod in the public eye with a load of genial respectability, and in a moment, like a schoolboy, strip off these lendings

alignments.same: Each relishes keeping a respectable face in society while living a hidden life of vice.
alignments.differs: Jekyll has to swallow a draught and become another body to slip free; Dorian dines in society with his own face the evening after a murder, and the calm is the pleasure.

from.exact: It was not till they had examined the rings that they recognized who it was.

to.exact: He was dressed in clothes far too large for him, clothes of the doctor’s bigness

alignments.same: The household gets into the locked room and finds a dead man whose face is not the one they knew, placed only by what he wears.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's people find Hyde's face in the doctor's clothes and no Jekyll; Dorian's find their master young on the wall and a withered body known by its rings.

question: Hyde lets Jekyll keep his good name by changing bodies; the portrait lets Dorian keep his face by taking his years and sins. Which bargain costs more, and who pays it?

substitution.note: With Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini's Daughter or The Birth-Mark in place of Jekyll and Hyde the claim fails: none has a respectable man whose sins are carried by a second shape of himself, and none ends with a household forcing a room to find a body known only by its clothes. No other book in the library sits under The double.

claim: Both tales call an old friend to a house where a man has shut his second self behind a door, and leave others listening to it move. Usher's double is a twin he buried alive, who breaks out and comes in to carry him down; Jekyll's is himself, and when his friends break in they find only Hyde.

from.exact: You are one of my oldest friends

to.exact: an earnest desire to see me, as his best, and indeed his only personal friend

alignments.same: A man in trouble writes to a friend of his youth and begs for his help.
alignments.differs: Usher asks his friend to come and cheer him in the house; Jekyll asks Lanyon to fetch a drawer of drugs and open his door at midnight to a stranger.

from.exact: that patient foot was still going up and down, up and down, in the quiet of the night

to.exact: I heard her first feeble movements in the hollow coffin

alignments.same: Someone listens through a shut door or lid to the shut-in other self moving.
alignments.differs: Utterson and Poole hear a stranger's step and fear their master is murdered; Usher hears the sister he entombed and, for days, dares not speak.

from.exact: the lock burst and the wreck of the door fell inwards on the carpet

to.exact: threw slowly back, upon the instant, their ponderous and ebony jaws

alignments.same: The door gives way and the hidden second self is in the room.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's friends break in with an axe and find Hyde dead and no Jekyll; Usher's doors open from without and his living twin comes in and bears him to the floor dead.

question: Usher keeps silent while his double struggles in the tomb; Jekyll writes everything down. Does confession save Jekyll anything that silence cost Usher?

substitution.note: With Dorian Gray in place of Jekyll and Hyde the claim fails: no friend is called by letter, nobody listens at a door to Dorian's other self, and the servants get in by the roof and the balcony. With Frankenstein in place of Usher it fails: Victor shuts nothing away behind a door, and the creature is neither his twin nor himself. Moreau, Rappaccini's Daughter and The Birth-Mark fail as well: none calls a friend by letter or shuts a second self of the hero away behind a door.

claim: Both tales bind a man to a made thing that shows his ruin and ends with him. Usher's house was cracked before he was born and, he believes, made him what he is; Dorian's portrait is marked by each sin he chooses. When the man dies, the house splits and sinks into the tarn, while the portrait hangs young again.

from.exact: For every sin that he committed, a stain would fleck and wreck its fairness.

to.exact: a barely perceptible fissure, which, extending from the roof of the building in front, made its way down the wall in a zigzag direction

alignments.same: The ruin of the man's other self first shows as a small mark on its surface.
alignments.differs: The fissure is in the house before the narrator arrives and belongs to the whole race; each stain on the portrait follows a sin Dorian has just committed.

from.exact: As it had revealed to him his own body, so it would reveal to him his own soul.

to.exact: which for centuries had moulded the destinies of his family, and which made him what I now saw him

alignments.same: A man believes a thing outside him is bound to his inner life.
alignments.differs: Usher thinks the stones of the house shaped him and his family; Dorian's deeds shape the picture, and he means to watch it as a mirror of his soul.

from.exact: a splendid portrait of their master as they had last seen him

to.exact: the deep and dank tarn at my feet closed sullenly and silently over the fragments

alignments.same: When the man dies, the thing that carried his ruin meets its end with him.
alignments.differs: The House of Usher splits and sinks with the last Usher; Dorian's portrait comes back young and whole, and the ruin passes to the dead body.

question: Usher blames the house for what he is; Dorian makes the portrait what it is. Which tale leaves its hero more to answer for?

substitution.note: With Jekyll and Hyde in place of Dorian Gray the claim fails: Hyde is a living body, not a made thing marked stain by stain, and nothing is left whole at the end. Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini's Daughter and The Birth-Mark fail too: no creature, beast-man, garden or mark shows the ruin of the man bound to it, and none falls or stands whole when he dies.

claim: Both tales send a doubting visitor into a house that works on whoever lives in it, and both end with the house brought down. Usher believes the stones themselves feel, and the whole house sinks with him; Bulwer's narrator traces the power to a distant man's will seated in a sealed room, so only that room is razed.

from.exact: my persuasion is, that they originate in some brain now far distant

to.exact: The conditions of the sentience had been here, he imagined, fulfilled in the method of collocation of these stones

alignments.same: A man sets out a theory of what in the house is working on the people inside it.
alignments.differs: Usher places the power in the stones, fungi and tarn themselves; Bulwer's narrator denies the house any power and places it in a human brain far away.

from.exact: It was closely nailed down, with clamps and rivets of iron.

to.exact: The door, of massive iron, had been, also, similarly protected.

alignments.same: Below the rooms lies a chamber shut with iron that holds the source of the horror.
alignments.differs: The narrator helps Usher lock a living twin in the vault, and she breaks out; Bulwer's narrator breaks in from above and finds only the phials, portrait and compass of a charlatan long fled.

from.exact: He razed to the foundations the part of the building containing the secret room with the chamber over it.

to.exact: the deep and dank tarn at my feet closed sullenly and silently over the fragments

alignments.same: The haunted building is torn down to its foundations at the end.
alignments.differs: Usher's house splits of itself and sinks with its master as the narrator flees; Mr. J—— pulls down one room on purpose, then lives in the house and lets it.

question: Usher's narrator calls the storm-light electrical and still flees; Bulwer's narrator calls the Thing natural and stays till dawn. What does each tale gain or lose by explaining its ghost?

substitution.note: With Jekyll and Hyde or Dorian Gray in place of Usher the claim fails: no visitor comes to a house said to work on its dwellers, and no house is brought down at the end. Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini's Daughter and The Birth-Mark fail too: Moreau's enclosure burns, but nobody holds that its stones or a will sealed in it shape the people inside, and none of the others has a haunted house at all.

claim: Both tales bring a man of plain science to a forced lock, phosphorus phials and a little book, then to a marvel he will not call supernatural. Bulwer's narrator explains it as a distant will, refuses to fear, and destroys its source; Lanyon, who scorned Jekyll's science, cannot explain what he saw and dies of it.

from.exact: seemed to me to contain phosphorus and some volatile ether

to.exact: phosphor and ammonia entered into some of them

alignments.same: After a lock is forced, a man examines another man's phials and finds phosphorus in a volatile liquid.
alignments.differs: Lanyon's phial belongs to a living friend and is drunk before his eyes that night; the crystal bottles belong to a charlatan who fled London in the last century and are never used.

from.exact: The book was an ordinary version book and contained little but a series of dates.

to.exact: it contained but one sheet of thick vellum

alignments.same: Beside the phials lies a small book that should tell what they were for.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's book logs years of experiments on himself and tells Lanyon little; the charlatan's vellum holds one curse that binds the house and all in it to his will.

from.exact: and yet I shall die incredulous

to.exact: Now, my theory is that the supernatural is the impossible

alignments.same: A man who trusts science sees a marvel and still will not grant that it is beyond nature.
alignments.differs: Lanyon finds no theory to hold what he saw and is dying of the shock; Bulwer's narrator fits the Thing into a theory of will and nerves, and his firmness keeps him alive.

question: Lanyon dies still doubting; Bulwer's narrator lives by his theory. Is it the theory that saves the narrator, or something the theory leaves out?

substitution.note: With Usher in place of The Haunted and the Haunters the claim fails: no lock is forced on phials and a book, and the narrator flees without a theory. Dorian Gray, Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini's Daughter and The Birth-Mark fail in place of either tale: Baglioni's vial and Aylmer's laboratory hold no book that should explain them, and no witness of plain science sees a marvel and either lives by a theory of it or dies refusing to believe it.

claim: Both tales send sceptics with a revolver and the language of psychical science to meet a ghost, and both end by opening a hidden room. Bulwer's ghost overpowers the narrator, who traces it to a living will and destroys its instruments; Wilde's Americans frighten the ghost instead, and he rests only when a child prays beside his chained bones.

from.exact: there were not even those primary conditions of receptive expectations which so often precede the presentation of psychical phenomena

to.exact: I was in as tranquil a temper for observation as any practical experimentalist could be

alignments.same: Before the ghost appears, the teller insists in scientific terms that the watchers' minds were not primed to see one.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's narrator works at calm, reading Macaulay against fancy; the Otises are calm because they talked of actresses and buckwheat cakes, and the report mocks the jargon.

from.exact: the United States Minister covered him with his revolver

to.exact: on the arm and shoulder I received a strange shock, and my arm fell to my side powerless

alignments.same: A man faces the ghost with the revolver he brought into the house.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's narrator cannot even reach his weapon, struck powerless by a will stronger than his; Mr. Otis aims his and orders the ghost to hold up his hands, and the ghost shrieks and flees.

from.exact: Imbedded in the wall was a huge iron ring, and chained to it was a gaunt skeleton

to.exact: we descended into a room below, the existence of which had never been suspected

alignments.same: At the end the living are led into a sealed room no one knew of and find what lay behind the haunting.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's room holds a charlatan's phials and curse, which are burned and the room razed; Virginia's holds the ghost's own starved body, over which she kneels and prays.

question: Bulwer's haunting ends when its source is found and destroyed; Wilde's ends when the ghost is pitied and forgiven. What does each tale think a ghost is?

substitution.note: With Usher in place of The Haunted and the Haunters the claim fails: Usher's narrator carries no weapon and sets no observer's calm against the ghost, and the vault is opened by the dead twin, not by the living. Jekyll and Dorian Gray have no haunted house and no ghost met by sceptics, so they fail in place of either tale.

claim: Both tales put a family house under a doom in verse, with a kinsman shut alive in its walls and a romance of chivalry read at night. In Usher the romance comes true as the buried twin breaks out and the house falls; in Canterville the romance's cock will not crow again, and a child's prayer makes the house still.

from.exact: There he consulted several books of ancient chivalry, of which he was exceedingly fond

to.exact: The antique volume which I had taken up was the “Mad Trist” of Sir Launcelot Canning

alignments.same: An old romance of knights is read in the house at night while its horror waits.
alignments.differs: Each sound in the Mad Trist is echoed in the house as Madeline breaks out; the ghost's books promise the cock will crow twice, it crows once, and his oath of blood comes to nothing.

from.exact: I don't think it was very nice of her brothers to starve me to death, though I did kill her.

to.exact: We have put her living in the tomb!

alignments.same: Kin shut a member of the family alive inside the house to die there.
alignments.differs: Roderick entombs his twin in fear and haste, and she returns within days to carry him down; Sir Simon's brothers-in-law starve him for murder, and he haunts three hundred years until he begs to die.

from.exact: Then shall all the house be still And peace come to Canterville.

to.exact: A hideous throng rush out forever, And laugh—but smile no more.

alignments.same: Verses within the tale tell what will become of the house and its family.
alignments.differs: Usher's ballad ends in a ruined palace that evil things never leave, and the house sinks; the window prophecy ends in stillness, fulfilled when the almond blossoms and the ghost is buried.

question: The Mad Trist comes true in Usher, and the books of chivalry fail the Canterville ghost. What does each tale do with the old romance it quotes?

substitution.note: With The Haunted and the Haunters in place of Usher the claim fails: its house has no verse prophecy, no kinsman shut in alive and no romance read aloud. Jekyll and Dorian Gray have no family house under a doom in verse, so they fail in place of either tale.

claim: Both tales leave a murderer with a red stain that will not stay clean and a plea to pray. Sir Simon repaints his stain, asks a child to pray for him, and is forgiven into a quiet grave; Dorian's stain spreads of itself, he answers Basil's plea with a knife, and stabbing the picture for peace, he dies.

from.exact: And why was the red stain larger than it had been?

to.exact: except to keep the blood-stain in proper repair

alignments.same: A murder leaves a red stain in the house that keeps coming back however it is cleaned.
alignments.differs: The ghost renews the stain himself, at last with a girl's stolen paints, to keep his crime on show; the stain on Dorian's picture grows of itself while he wants every trace gone.

from.exact: “Pray, Dorian, pray,” he murmured.

to.exact: you must weep with me for my sins, because I have no tears, and pray with me for my soul, because I have no faith

alignments.same: Someone asks for prayer over a murderer's sins.
alignments.differs: The ghost begs a child to pray for him, and she does; Basil begs Dorian to pray with him, and Dorian kills him.

from.exact: without its hideous warnings, he would be at peace

to.exact: To forget time, to forget life, to be at peace.

alignments.same: A man burdened with an old murder longs for peace.
alignments.differs: Sir Simon asks for death and gets it by a child's prayer and tears; Dorian seeks peace by killing the picture that is his conscience, and the knife kills him.

question: The ghost keeps his blood-stain painted; Dorian wants his stain gone. Which of them is closer to repentance?

substitution.note: With Jekyll and Hyde in place of either tale the claim fails: Jekyll leaves no red stain and no one asks him to pray. The Birth-Mark has a red mark that will not come off, but on a living wife, with no murder behind it and no plea to pray; Usher, The Haunted and the Haunters, Frankenstein, Moreau and Rappaccini's Daughter have no murderer begged to pray and no returning stain, so they fail in place of The Canterville Ghost.

claim: Both tales bring a ghost who did evil in life to children in an English country house, and leave a child silent about it. Wilde's girl goes with the ghost, prays him into rest and keeps her secret; James's governess tries to force the ghosts' names from her pupils, and the boy who speaks one dies in her arms.

from.exact: Of the lost. Of the damned. And that’s why, to share them—

to.exact: for against the purity of a little child the powers of Hell cannot prevail

alignments.same: A dead sinner is said to need a living child, and the child's soul is what is at stake.
alignments.differs: Sir Simon needs Virginia's purity to win his own rest and promises Hell cannot touch her; the governess believes Miss Jessel wants Flora to share her torments.

from.exact: I don’t know what you mean. I see nobody. I see nothing. I never have.

to.exact: "I have never told any one, Cecil," said Virginia, gravely.

alignments.same: A girl who has been near the ghost will not tell the grown-ups what passed.
alignments.differs: Virginia owns that she was with the ghost and is trusted to keep its secret; Flora denies there was anything to see, and the governess takes the denial as proof that she is lost.

from.exact: but he has lost you forever!

to.exact: I have been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him.

alignments.same: The struggle over a child ends with a death and the ghost gone for good.
alignments.differs: At Canterville the ghost dies at peace and the girl comes back with his jewels; at Bly the governess cries that the ghost has lost the boy, and it is the boy who dies.

question: Virginia's silence is trusted and Flora's is not. What makes the governess sure that a child who sees nothing is hiding something?

substitution.note: With Usher or The Haunted and the Haunters in place of The Canterville Ghost the claim fails: no child meets the ghost there and none keeps silent about it. Dorian, Jekyll, Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini's Daughter and The Birth-Mark have no ghost and no child, so they fail too.

claim: Both tales bring an outsider to a lonely house to stand by the last of a family, and both tellers own that imagination was at work before the horror came. Usher begs his friend by letter, and his buried sister carries him down dead; James's master forbids the governess to write, and the boy dies in her arms.

from.exact: That she should never trouble him—but never, never: neither appeal nor complain nor write about anything

to.exact: which, in its wildly importunate nature, had admitted of no other than a personal reply

alignments.same: The head of the house hands an outsider the care of the family's trouble.
alignments.differs: Usher's letter begs his friend to come and share his terror; the master in Harley Street takes the governess on condition that she never write to him at all.

from.exact: my imagination had, in a flash, turned real

to.exact: I had so worked upon my imagination as really to believe

alignments.same: The teller admits that imagination was at work just before the house first shows its horror.
alignments.differs: Poe's narrator calls his fancy a dream and shakes it off until the house proves it; the governess's daydream of meeting the master becomes a stranger on the tower whom only she sees.

from.exact: his little heart, dispossessed, had stopped

to.exact: bore him to the floor a corpse, and a victim to the terrors he had anticipated

alignments.same: The tale ends with the last male heir dead in someone's grip as the haunting reaches its height.
alignments.differs: Madeline is a body that breaks out of the vault and falls on her brother; Miles dies held by the governess while the ghost stands at a window he cannot see.

question: Poe's narrator catches Usher's fear; the governess may be passing hers to Miles. In each house, who is the source of the terror?

substitution.note: With The Haunted and the Haunters in place of Usher the claim fails: its narrator comes on his own, with no family to stand by, and no one dies in his grip. The Canterville Ghost has no outsider teller and no death in anyone's arms; in Jekyll, Utterson is a friend and Hyde dies alone behind a locked door. Dorian, Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini's Daughter and The Birth-Mark have no summons to a family house.

claim: Both tales set a beautiful boy whose face defeats every evil report beside an older man blamed for spoiling him. Wilde names the book that poisoned Dorian and hangs his sins on a hidden picture; James never shows what Quint taught Miles, and the governess, finding no guilt in his face, comes to read the beauty as the fraud.

from.exact: It would have been impossible to carry a bad name with a greater sweetness of innocence

to.exact: could not believe anything to his dishonour when they saw him

alignments.same: An evil report about a beautiful young man is set aside by those who see his face.
alignments.differs: Dorian's face stays clean because the portrait bears his sins; Miles's face makes the governess lock the school's letter in a drawer, and its charge is never cleared.

from.exact: Their more than earthly beauty, their absolutely unnatural goodness. It’s a game

to.exact: Sin is a thing that writes itself across a man’s face. It cannot be concealed.

alignments.same: A watcher states a rule for reading vice in a beautiful face.
alignments.differs: Basil holds that sin must show, so a pure face proves innocence; the governess decides that the children's beauty and goodness are themselves the mask of guilt.

from.exact: Quint was much too free.

to.exact: Yet you poisoned me with a book once.

alignments.same: An older man is blamed for spoiling a beautiful youth.
alignments.differs: Dorian names Lord Henry and the book; at Bly Quint's part is only hinted by the housekeeper, and Miles owns no more than that he 'said things'.

question: Basil cannot believe the rumours once he sees Dorian; the governess ends by distrusting Miles because of his beauty. Which way of reading a face does each book bear out?

substitution.note: With Jekyll and Hyde in place of Dorian the claim fails: Hyde's face shows his evil and no one is blamed for spoiling him. Rappaccini's Daughter has a beautiful poisoned girl and a father to blame, but no book and no hidden picture; Canterville, Usher, The Haunted and the Haunters, Frankenstein, Moreau and The Birth-Mark have no beautiful youth under an evil report.

claim: Both tales shut a nervous invalid in an old house that works on the mind, with a woman behind a wall who struggles out and a man who falls before her. Usher's buried sister bears him down dead; Gilman's teller, whose doctor husband calls her hardly sick, becomes the woman behind the paper herself, and the husband faints.

from.exact: temporary nervous depression—a slight hysterical tendency

to.exact: a mere nervous affection, he immediately added, which would undoubtedly soon pass off

alignments.same: A grave illness is called a passing nervous complaint.
alignments.differs: Usher plays down his own family evil in the same breath that he despairs of a remedy; in Gilman the husband-physician makes the diagnosis, and the patient writes that she disagrees.

from.exact: This paper looks to me as if it knew what a vicious influence it had!

to.exact: some peculiarities in the mere form and substance of his family mansion

alignments.same: The sufferer believes the fabric of the house has an influence over the mind.
alignments.differs: Usher means the stones of his forefathers, which have shaped his family for centuries; Gilman's teller means the paper of one rented room, and no one but she believes it.

from.exact: Now why should that man have fainted?

to.exact: bore him to the floor a corpse

alignments.same: The woman shut away comes out, and the man of the house falls to the floor before her.
alignments.differs: Madeline falls on her brother and both die while the guest flees; Gilman's woman is the teller herself, unhurt, who keeps creeping over her fainted husband.

question: Usher's sister breaks out of the tomb her brother put her in; Gilman's teller frees a woman from the wallpaper and finds that it is herself. Who is buried in each house, and by whom?

substitution.note: The Turn of the Screw has a lonely house and a frightened woman teller, but no one is shut behind a wall and the one who falls is a child. Jekyll and Hyde has a locked room and a second self, but no woman and no house that works on the mind. The Haunted and the Haunters and Canterville have houses that act on their tenants but no confined woman breaking out. The Birth-Mark has a husband's diagnosis and a secluded wife, but no house and no one breaking out. Dorian, Frankenstein, Moreau and Rappaccini have none of the three.

claim: Both tales seclude a wife under her husband's science for a cure needing perfect rest, and fix eyes at dawn on a mark that shifts with the light. Aylmer watches the mark on Georgiana's cheek; she drinks his cure in trust and dies; Gilman's wife watches the paper herself, comes to fear her doctor, and it is he who falls.

from.exact: that I was to have perfect rest and all the air I could get

to.exact: would enjoy the perfect repose essential to its success

alignments.same: A husband of science moves his wife into a room set apart for a cure that needs perfect rest.
alignments.differs: Aylmer hangs curtains and shuts out the sun to make her an enchanted boudoir; John takes the barred nursery at the top of the house, with windows that look all ways.

from.exact: When the sun shoots in through the east window—I always watch for that first long, straight ray

to.exact: With the morning twilight Aylmer opened his eyes upon his wife’s face and recognized the symbol of imperfection

alignments.same: At dawn someone looks first for a mark that changes with the light.
alignments.differs: In Hawthorne the husband watches the mark on his wife's face; in Gilman the wife watches the mark on the wall, a fancy her husband's science forbids.

from.exact: I am a doctor, dear, and I know.

to.exact: Unless all my science have deceived me, it cannot fail.

alignments.same: The husband vouches for the cure on the strength of his science.
alignments.differs: Georgiana answers by drinking the draught that kills her; Gilman's wife falls silent before the doctor but goes on watching, and comes to be afraid of him.

question: Georgiana drinks Aylmer's cure because she trusts him; Gilman's teller stops arguing with John but keeps watching the paper. Which wife resists her husband's science, and what does resisting cost her?

substitution.note: Rappaccini's Daughter has a secluded woman and a cure that kills, but the man of science is her father, not her husband, and no one watches a changing mark. Frankenstein, Moreau, Jekyll and Dorian have men of science or art but no wife put under a rest cure. Usher has a sick woman and her physicians, but no husband and no cure. The Turn of the Screw, The Haunted and the Haunters and Canterville have no husband's science at all.

claim: Both tales let a second self shake loose from its prison and take over a writer who hides the pages, and end with a man at a locked door crying for an axe. Jekyll's drug frees his own evil, and the axe finds Hyde dead; Gilman's wife frees the woman in the wallpaper and becomes her, and her husband faints.

from.exact: she just takes hold of the bars and shakes them hard

to.exact: it but shook the doors of the prisonhouse of my disposition

alignments.same: A self held behind bars is shaken loose.
alignments.differs: Jekyll's drug shakes the prison and his own evil runs out as Hyde; Gilman's woman shakes the bars herself, and the teller who helps her out ends as that woman.

from.exact: There comes John, and I must put this away,—he hates to have me write a word.

to.exact: Should the throes of change take me in the act of writing it, Hyde will tear it in pieces

alignments.same: The one writing hurries to keep the pages from someone who would stop them.
alignments.differs: Jekyll fears his other self will destroy his confession; Gilman's wife hides her journal from her husband, who forbids her work for her health.

from.exact: Now he’s crying for an axe.

to.exact: Poole swung the axe over his shoulder

alignments.same: A man outside a locked room calls for an axe to reach the one changed inside.
alignments.differs: Poole breaks the door and they find Hyde dead and Jekyll gone; John is told where the key lies, opens the door, finds his wife alive and creeping, and faints.

question: Jekyll writes that Hyde is the evil in him set free; Gilman's teller says she has got out at last. Is the self each one releases a prisoner or a jailer?

substitution.note: Dorian Gray has a hidden second self and a locked room, but no one writes in secret and the servants climb in by the roof. Usher has a woman breaking out of a vault, but no writer hiding pages and no axe; the doors open in the wind. The Turn of the Screw has a woman writing at a lonely house, but no second self set free and no locked door. Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini, The Birth-Mark, The Haunted and the Haunters and Canterville have no second self that takes over the writer.

claim: Both tales leave a young woman in a lonely country house, under a man's rule not to write or complain, who alone sees a woman's figure there. Gilman's wife keeps the figure secret and becomes her; James's governess needs others to see the ghost to prove she is sane, and no one will say they do.

from.exact: neither appeal nor complain nor write about anything

to.exact: am absolutely forbidden to “work” until I am well again

alignments.same: The man over a young woman forbids her to write.
alignments.differs: The master asks for silence so that he is never troubled, and the governess keeps it out of pride; John forbids his wife's work for her health, and she writes in secret anyway.

from.exact: an insane, an unmentionable relative kept in unsuspected confinement

to.exact: it becomes bars! The outside pattern I mean, and the woman behind it is as plain as can be

alignments.same: The house is thought to hold a woman kept behind bars.
alignments.differs: James's governess raises a madwoman in confinement only as a guess and drops it; Gilman's wife sees the barred woman every night, and the confinement is her own.

from.exact: she was there, and I was neither cruel nor mad

to.exact: I am determined that nobody shall find it out but myself!

alignments.same: A woman alone sees a figure no one else will own to seeing.
alignments.differs: The governess wants Mrs. Grose and Flora to see Miss Jessel as proof that she is sane; Gilman's wife wants no one else to see the woman, and hides what she knows.

question: The governess needs a witness to prove she is not mad; Gilman's teller wants none. Does either story let us decide whether the woman seen is there?

substitution.note: Usher, The Haunted and the Haunters and Canterville have houses that work on those inside, but their tellers are men or the tale is told from outside, and no woman alone sees a woman's figure. Jekyll, Dorian, Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini and The Birth-Mark have no woman who sees what others will not own to seeing.

claim: Both tales bring a guest to an old house on a stormy night, where events seem to follow a romance read or told beforehand, and a woman may lie alive in the family vault. Catherine finds a washing-bill and a wife truly dead, and wakes ashamed; Usher's sister was buried alive, and comes out to carry him down.

from.exact: the exact counterpart of what my fancy had already conjured up

to.exact: this striking exemplification of what Henry had foretold

alignments.same: On a stormy night in an old house, what happens matches, point for point, a romance just read or told.
alignments.differs: Poe's sounds truly come from the buried Madeline breaking out; Catherine's cabinet matches Henry's joke only because she looks for the match, and its roll is a washing-bill.

from.exact: We have put her living in the tomb!

to.exact: Were she even to descend into the family vault where her ashes were supposed to slumber

alignments.same: A woman of the house is thought to lie in the family vault while she may still be alive.
alignments.differs: Usher's sister was truly laid living in the vault, and he heard her and kept silent; Catherine fancies Mrs. Tilney's coffin a sham, but the wife died of a fever.

from.exact: a victim to the terrors he had anticipated

to.exact: a mind which, before she entered the abbey, had been craving to be frightened

alignments.same: The fear is made ready before any horror comes.
alignments.differs: Usher's anticipated terror arrives in his sister's body and kills him; Catherine's craved terror never comes, and she sees she made it from her reading.

question: Poe's narrator and Catherine both match what they hear to a story they know. What decides, in each tale, whether the match is fancy or truth?

substitution.note: Turn of the Screw guesses at a hidden relative but has no vault and no romance read on a stormy night; Canterville reads a romance at night but its walled-up kinsman is a man and long dead. Haunted, Yellow Wallpaper, Jekyll, Dorian and the A1 works have no woman of the house thought alive in a tomb.

claim: Both tales lodge a young woman who knows her Udolpho in a great country house, where she guesses at a relative kept locked away and is told nothing is there. Henry's rebuke wakes Catherine to her own delusion; James's governess finds her imagination turned real, refuses Mrs. Grose's denial, and the boy dies in her arms.

from.exact: a mystery of Udolpho or an insane, an unmentionable relative kept in unsuspected confinement

to.exact: the probability that Mrs. Tilney yet lived, shut up for causes unknown

alignments.same: A young woman in a great country house guesses, as in Udolpho, that a relative is kept locked away there.
alignments.differs: Catherine builds the guess into a nightly plot against the General's wife and acts on it; the governess raises it once and drops it, for she has seen a man on the tower.

from.exact: my imagination had, in a flash, turned real

to.exact: it had been all a voluntary, self-created delusion

alignments.same: The heroine owns that her imagination ran ahead of what she met.
alignments.differs: Catherine learns that nothing answered her fancy and calls it self-made; the governess says her fancy came true on the tower, and never takes it back.

from.exact: She isn’t there, little lady, and nobody’s there

to.exact: Consult your own understanding, your own sense of the probable

alignments.same: Someone of the household tells the young woman that the horror she sees is not there.
alignments.differs: Henry's appeal to sense sends Catherine off in tears of shame and cures her; Mrs. Grose's denial only proves to the governess that Flora has been turned against her.

question: Henry Tilney talks Catherine out of her fears; nobody can talk the governess out of hers. Is James's governess a Catherine whom no Henry reached, or does James give her reasons Austen never gives Catherine?

substitution.note: Yellow Wallpaper has a woman told her fancies are nothing, but she is a wife at home, knows no Udolpho and guesses at no relative confined. Usher, Haunted and Canterville have no young woman guessing at a hidden relative; Jekyll, Dorian and the A1 works have no country-house guest corrected by the household.

claim: Both tales bring visitors from modern life to an old English house where a husband is said to have destroyed his wife. Catherine expects horrors, finds a Rumford grate, and her charge against the General proves false; the Otises expect nothing, scrub the murdered wife's blood with a patent cleaner, and the husband's ghost keeps coming back.

from.exact: who was murdered on that very spot by her own husband

to.exact: who must have been in some way or other her destroyer

alignments.same: The old house is said to keep the memory of a wife destroyed by her husband.
alignments.differs: Catherine charges the General on no evidence and is proved wrong; Wilde's housekeeper tells of a true murder, and the husband's ghost still walks.

from.exact: Pinkerton's Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent

to.exact: was contracted to a Rumford

alignments.same: Modern manufacture stands where the visitor's Gothic house should be.
alignments.differs: At Northanger the General has already modernised the abbey and Catherine is sorry; Washington Otis scrubs the old stain with a patent cleaner, and it comes back every morning.

from.exact: a fearful peal of thunder made them all start to their feet

to.exact: it had wafted nothing worse than a thick mizzling rain

alignments.same: Weather meets the newcomers as they arrive at the old house.
alignments.differs: Austen's rain brings no omen, and Catherine thinks only of her bonnet; Wilde's thunder answers the scrubbing of the blood as if on cue, and the housekeeper faints.

question: Austen's heroine believes in Gothic horror and the house disappoints her; Wilde's family disbelieves and the house insists. Which tale takes the Gothic less seriously?

substitution.note: Usher, Haunted and Turn of the Screw bring outsiders to old houses, but none tells of a husband who killed his wife or meets the Gothic with modern goods. Dorian has a murderer and a stain but no visitors to an old house; Yellow Wallpaper, Jekyll and the A1 works have no wife murdered by her husband.

claim: Both tales leave a guest alone overnight in a house of dark report, steadying the mind against fear, and put old papers from a drawer in the guest's hands. Bulwer's letters hint at a crime, and an inquiry finds a child let die for money; Catherine's roll is a washing-bill, and Henry's account of his mother's fever clears his father.

from.exact: I fully determined to keep my mind in a fit state to cope with whatever of marvellous the advancing night might bring forth

to.exact: Thus wisely fortifying her mind

alignments.same: Alone at night in a house of dark repute, the sleeper resolves to keep a steady mind.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's narrator holds firm while real wonders come; Catherine's resolve breaks when she snuffs out her candle, though nothing comes but wind.

from.exact: two letters tied round with a narrow ribbon of faded yellow

to.exact: her quick eyes directly fell on a roll of paper

alignments.same: Searching a drawer by candlelight, the guest finds old papers put away out of sight.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's letters are thirty-five years old and hint at a secret crime; Catherine's roll is in modern characters and lists linen.

from.exact: he had instituted a cautious inquiry about the woman

to.exact: On the fifth day she died.

alignments.same: An account of how someone of the house died answers the guest's suspicion.
alignments.differs: Mr. J——'s inquiry finds a child neglected to death for an inheritance; Henry's account of physicians and a bilious fever clears his father.

question: Bulwer's papers lead to a real crime and Austen's to a laundry list. What does each tale want its reader to feel about a guest who goes through the drawers?

substitution.note: Usher, Canterville and Turn of the Screw have guests in old houses, but none finds old papers in a drawer at night that lead to an account of a death. Yellow Wallpaper, Jekyll, Dorian and the A1 works have no guest searching a strange room's drawers.

claim: Both tales lay a young woman in a family vault while she seems still alive, and bring her out to claim the man nearest her. Usher heard his twin stir and dared not speak, and she bears him down dead; Stoker's men open Lucy's coffin themselves, and her lover answers her call with the stake that gives her rest.

from.exact: Has there been any mistake; has she been buried alive?

to.exact: We have put her living in the tomb!

alignments.same: A man who loved the dead woman fears she was laid living in the tomb.
alignments.differs: Usher's fear is true, and he heard her stir for days in silence; Arthur is told Lucy is not alive but Un-Dead, and the men will open the coffin.

from.exact: more rose and more beautiful in a whole week, after she die

to.exact: the mockery of a faint blush upon the bosom and the face

alignments.same: The woman in the coffin keeps the colour of life on her face.
alignments.differs: Madeline's blush is the mark of a trance and she still lives; Lucy's bloom grows after death, while children are found wounded by the churchyard.

from.exact: Come to me, Arthur. Leave these others and come to me.

to.exact: fell heavily inward upon the person of her brother

alignments.same: The woman out of the tomb comes for the man closest to her.
alignments.differs: Madeline falls on her brother and bears him to the floor dead; Van Helsing's crucifix bars Lucy from Arthur's arms, and Arthur drives the stake.

question: Usher dared not speak of what he heard below; Stoker's men go down and open the coffin. What does each tale make of the men who stand outside the tomb?

substitution.note: Northanger fancies a wife alive in the vault but she died of a fever, and no one comes out; Canterville's walled-up kinsman is a man, long dead. Turn of the Screw, Haunted, Yellow Wallpaper, Jekyll, Dorian, Werther and the A1 works lay no woman in a vault who returns.

claim: Both tales give a man of many crimes a face that does not age, and show him smashing a mirror. Dorian stays young because a portrait bears his years; the Count casts no reflection and grows young on others' blood. At death the body of each gives up its stolen years at once.

from.exact: It is a foul bauble of man’s vanity. Away with it!

to.exact: flinging the mirror on the floor, crushed it into silver splinters beneath his heel

alignments.same: A man whose youth is unnatural destroys a looking-glass in anger.
alignments.differs: The Count, who casts no reflection, flings out the glass that made Jonathan cut himself; Dorian crushes his own mirror because it shows the beauty that ruined him.

from.exact: I believe it is the Count, but he has grown young.

to.exact: the fair young face that laughed back at him from the polished glass

alignments.same: A man's face stays or grows young while he lives by evil.
alignments.differs: Dorian's youth is kept by a hidden picture that ages in his place; the Count's is renewed by blood drunk from others, and Jonathan sees it in a Piccadilly street.

from.exact: the whole body crumbled into dust and passed from our sight

to.exact: He was withered, wrinkled, and loathsome of visage.

alignments.same: At the moment of death the body loses the youth it kept.
alignments.differs: Dorian's corpse takes the portrait's ruin and is known only by its rings; the Count's crumbles to dust in a breath, and Mina sees a look of peace on his face.

question: Dorian keeps a picture that ages for him; the Count has no image in the glass at all. What does each tale make a mirror show about a man who will not age?

substitution.note: Jekyll has a mirror and a second shape but no unageing face; Canterville's ghost is centuries old but grows no younger and breaks no mirror. Usher, Haunted, Turn of the Screw, Yellow Wallpaper, Northanger, Werther and the A1 works keep no man young against his crimes.

claim: Both tales set a man of science weighing vivisection against conscience, beside a creature drawn to eat living flesh, and both speak of blood passed by surgery from body to body. Moreau follows his question and never minds the ethics; Seward stops himself before experimenting on Renfield, and the transfusions are men's own blood given to save Lucy.

from.exact: Men sneered at vivisection, and yet look at its results to-day!

to.exact: To this day I have never troubled about the ethics of the matter

alignments.same: A man of science sets vivisection against the scruples of others.
alignments.differs: Seward pleads its results and then warns himself not to be tempted to experiment on Renfield; Moreau needs no results and never troubled about ethics at all.

from.exact: call him a zoöphagous (life-eating) maniac

to.exact: Not to eat Flesh or Fish; that is the Law.

alignments.same: A creature watched by men of science is drawn to eat living flesh.
alignments.differs: Moreau's beasts chant a law against flesh and slip back to it; Renfield is a man who climbs from flies to spiders to birds, and Seward only names a new class.

from.exact: to transfer from full veins of one to the empty veins which pine for him

to.exact: The memory of his work on the transfusion of blood recurred to me.

alignments.same: A doctor is known for passing blood from one body into another.
alignments.differs: Prendick takes Moreau's transfusions for part of a hideous experiment on victims; Van Helsing's take blood from Lucy's lover and friends to save her from the creature who drinks it.

question: Seward warns himself off experimenting on Renfield unless there is 'a sufficient cause'; Moreau asks for none. What, in each book, holds back a doctor's knife?

substitution.note: Frankenstein, Birth-Mark and Rappaccini have men of science but no vivisection, no flesh-eating patient and no transfusion; Jekyll's Lanyon is a doctor who refuses Jekyll's science. Usher, Haunted, Canterville, Turn of the Screw, Yellow Wallpaper, Northanger, Dorian and Werther have none of the three.

claim: Both tales set men who trust mesmerism against a will that works on minds from afar, and end the evil by destroying the place it works from. Bulwer's narrator calls the power natural, and a sealed room is razed; Van Helsing turns Seward's faith in hypnotism toward the Un-Dead, follows the Count through Mina's trance, and still must kill him.

from.exact: how you accept the hypnotism and reject the thought reading

to.exact: my theory is that the supernatural is the impossible

alignments.same: A man of science who admits mesmerism draws the line of the possible.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's narrator stretches natural law to cover any ghost and stays a sceptic; Van Helsing turns Seward's belief in Charcot against him, to bring him to believe in the vampire.

from.exact: compel her mind to disclose to him that which she know

to.exact: conveyed to me from a distance by a human being who had acquired power over me by previous rapport

alignments.same: A distant will holds a mind through a bond made earlier.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's narrator offers the bond as a theory of his haunting; the Count's bond with Mina is blood drunk both ways, and the hunters turn it to follow him home.

from.exact: sterilise the earth, so that no more he can seek safety in it

to.exact: He razed to the foundations the part of the building containing the secret room

alignments.same: The men destroy the place from which the power works.
alignments.differs: Razing one room ends Bulwer's haunting, and the house is let; Stoker's men must sterilise box after box across London and still hunt the Count to his castle.

question: Bulwer's narrator explains his ghost by mesmerism and stays unafraid; Van Helsing uses mesmerism as a weapon. Does Stoker's book side with the sceptic or answer him?

substitution.note: Usher, Canterville, Turn of the Screw and Northanger have houses of dark report but no mesmerist and no will acting at a distance; Jekyll and Frankenstein have science but no mesmerism. Yellow Wallpaper, Dorian, Moreau, Rappaccini, Birth-Mark and Werther set no distant will on a mind.

claim: Both tales shut a narrator in an old house of ill report with a recluse of morbid acuteness, reading together through shuttered days. Usher's acuteness turns inward: he hears his buried sister and dies as the house falls. Dupin carries his into the night streets and the newspapers, and reasons from what others heard to a material killer.

from.exact: a time-eaten and grotesque mansion, long deserted through superstitions into which we did not inquire, and tottering to its fall

to.exact: He was enchained by certain superstitious impressions in regard to the dwelling which he tenanted

alignments.same: Two men share a decaying house that carries superstitions about it.
alignments.differs: Usher is bound to his family's house and its influence; Dupin and the narrator rent a stranger's ruin and do not ask what the superstitions are.

from.exact: By the aid of these we then busied our souls in dreams—reading, writing, or conversing

to.exact: We painted and read together

alignments.same: Narrator and friend pass their days shut in together over books.
alignments.differs: Usher never leaves his house; Dupin and the narrator go out arm in arm each night to watch the city.

from.exact: in whose tones, even, denizens of the five great divisions of Europe could recognise nothing familiar

to.exact: Said I not that my senses were acute?

alignments.same: A sound heard through walls and on stairs holds the secret of the horror.
alignments.differs: Usher heard the sound himself and dared not speak; Dupin heard nothing, and reasons from the witnesses' clashing reports to a voice that is no man's.

question: Poe lodges Dupin in a house much like Usher's and gives him the same nervous acuteness. What does analysis do with that temperament that Usher could not?

substitution.note: Haunted, Canterville, Turn of the Screw and Northanger have houses of dark report but no recluse who shares them with the narrator over books; Jekyll's friend lives apart from Utterson. Yellow Wallpaper, Dracula, Dorian, Frankenstein, Moreau, Rappaccini, Birth-Mark and Werther have no pair of companions shut in together.

claim: Both tales make a motiveless, ape-like killing the riddle and set listeners at a shut door to name a voice. Dupin reasons past the madman to a real ape that has no guilt to hide. Utterson's plain and natural explanation, a disfiguring illness, fails, and the ape-like killer is the respectable doctor himself.

from.exact: with ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim under foot

to.exact: a ferocity brutal, a butchery without motive

alignments.same: A savage killing without motive, beyond the cruelty of ordinary criminals.
alignments.differs: Poe's brutality proves to be a real orang-outang's; Stevenson's 'ape-like' fury is a simile for a gentleman's other self.

from.exact: Ah, that’s not Jekyll’s voice—it’s Hyde’s!

to.exact: each one spoke of it as that of a foreigner

alignments.same: Men at a closed door try to say whose voice is speaking inside.
alignments.differs: Poe's witnesses cannot place the voice in any nation and it is no man's; Utterson names a second man, and it is the master's own.

from.exact: There is my explanation; it is sad enough, Poole, ay, and appalling to consider; but it is plain and natural

to.exact: But the voices of madmen, even in their wildest paroxysms, are never found to tally with that peculiar voice

alignments.same: A medical explanation, madness or a disfiguring illness, is offered for the strange voice.
alignments.differs: Dupin rejects the madman and is right; Utterson holds to his natural explanation and is wrong, because the truth is stranger, not plainer.

question: In Poe the inhuman voice belongs to an animal and the case is closed; in Stevenson it belongs to the doctor. What does Stevenson keep from the detective story, and what does he refuse it?

substitution.note: Usher, Haunted and Turn of the Screw have listeners at doors but no murder to solve; Dracula and Moreau have brute violence but no voice behind a locked door named by witnesses; Dorian has a murder but no inquiry. The others have no murder.

claim: Both tales set beside men an ape that copies them and dreads the punishment they taught it. Poe's orang-outang copies its master's razor, kills, hides its deed for fear of the whip, and is sold to a menagerie. Wells's Ape-man copies speech without sense, recites the House of Pain, and follows Prendick home in the faces of Londoners.

from.exact: go off repeating it, with a word wrong here or there

to.exact: in which it had no doubt previously watched its master through the key-hole of the closet

alignments.same: An ape copies what it has seen or heard a man do.
alignments.differs: Poe's ape copies a razor stroke and the copy becomes murder; Wells's Ape-man copies words without their sense and passes them round as wisdom.

from.exact: I did a little thing, a wrong thing, once. I jabbered, jabbered, stopped talking.

to.exact: Conscious of having deserved punishment, it seemed desirous of concealing its bloody deeds

alignments.same: The ape fears a punishment its master has taught it.
alignments.differs: Poe's ape hides the bodies for fear of the whip, with no law to name; Wells's Ape-man has learnt a Law and speaks of his branding.

from.exact: it seemed that the preacher gibbered “Big Thinks,” even as the Ape-man had done

to.exact: who obtained for it a very large sum at the Jardin des Plantes

alignments.same: After the ape is gone, the narrator places it in the human world.
alignments.differs: Poe's ape is caged and sold and the case is closed; Prendick, home in London, hears the Ape-man in a preacher.

question: Poe's ape kills because it imitates; Wells's Ape-man is harmless but makes imitation look like human speech. Which tale is more troubled by how near the ape stands to man?

substitution.note: Only Jekyll among the others has an ape, and only as a simile; Frankenstein's creature learns speech but is no ape and is not punished into a law. Dracula, Usher and the rest have no imitating animal.

claim: Both tales set reasoners before attacks that seem beyond a man: a climb down a sheer wall, wounds no common assailant makes. Dupin rules out spirits and proves a sailor's escaped ape. Stoker gives that answer to a hospital doctor, while Van Helsing calls it the fault of science to explain all and leads Seward to the tomb.

from.exact: it is the fault of our science that it wants to explain all

to.exact: It is not too much to say that neither of us believe in præternatural events.

alignments.same: The investigator says what reason may admit before he names the attacker.
alignments.differs: Dupin rules out spirits at the start and the case yields to reason; Van Helsing blames science for explaining all away, and the attacker is Un-Dead.

from.exact: Some sailor may have brought one home, and it managed to escape

to.exact: The owner (who is ascertained to be a sailor, belonging to a Maltese vessel)

alignments.same: An animal a sailor brought home and lost is offered as the cause of the attacks.
alignments.differs: In Poe the sailor's runaway beast is the true answer; in Stoker it is a hospital doctor's guess about a bat, and Van Helsing answers it by taking Seward to Lucy's tomb.

from.exact: begin to crawl down the castle wall over that dreadful abyss, face down

to.exact: it perceived the lightning rod, clambered up with inconceivable agility

alignments.same: Something goes up or down the sheer wall of a building by a feat no man could do.
alignments.differs: Dupin proves the ape's climb possible and natural; Harker cannot believe what he sees, and the Count's crawl, face down, is the first sign he is no man.

question: The hospital doctor's escaped-animal theory is Dupin's solution. Is Stoker parodying the detective story, or asking his readers to hold its reason and his monster at once?

substitution.note: Haunted has a sceptic but no attacks and no escaped animal; Jekyll and Moreau have beasts or beast-like men but no reasoner who rules out the supernatural. Usher, Canterville, Turn of the Screw, Northanger, Yellow Wallpaper and the rest have no killing to explain.

claim: Both tales send a searcher through every drawer of a cabinet, alert to false linings, for a paper someone must have hidden. Catherine finds a hidden roll and it is a washing-bill: the secret was in her reading. The Prefect finds nothing, because the Minister made the real letter look like waste and left it in plain view.

from.exact: to a properly trained police agent, such a thing as a secret drawer is impossible

to.exact: Well read in the art of concealing a treasure, the possibility of false linings to the drawers did not escape her

alignments.same: A searcher opens every drawer and checks for secret drawers and false linings, sure a paper lies hidden there.
alignments.differs: Catherine's method comes from novels and her inner cavity does yield a roll of paper; the Prefect's comes from police rules and finds nothing at all.

from.exact: This last was much soiled and crumpled.

to.exact: An inventory of linen, in coarse and modern characters, seemed all that was before her!

alignments.same: The paper that counts looks, or proves to be, a worthless scrap.
alignments.differs: Catherine's precious manuscript really is a washing-bill; the Minister makes the precious letter look like waste, soiled and torn, so that searchers pass it by.

from.exact: escape observation by dint of being excessively obvious

to.exact: Or that she should be the first to possess the skill of unlocking a cabinet, the key of which was open to all!

alignments.same: What stands open to everyone is judged to hold no secret.
alignments.differs: For Catherine that judgment is the cure for her fancies; for Dupin it is the error the Minister counted on, and the open card-rack is the hiding place.

question: Catherine is cured by learning that the hidden paper was trivial; Dupin wins by suspecting a paper that only looks trivial. What does each tale teach its reader about where to look?

substitution.note: Haunted and the Haunters has a narrator open drawers and take two letters, but by chance, not a search for a hidden paper; Rue Morgue's police search a room for an exit, not a document. No other work has a drawer-by-drawer search for a hidden paper that turns out trivial or disguised as trivial.

claim: Both tales turn on a letter taken from a table to get a hold over its writer, and a questioner who reads the taker's mind. Dupin takes it back from the Minister unseen and leaves him to his ruin. The governess wrings from Miles that he took hers, found nothing in it and burned it, and her victory loses him.

from.exact: from the table in the hall, you took, you know, my letter

to.exact: he takes also from the table the letter to which he had no claim

alignments.same: A letter left on a table is taken by someone who has designs on its writer, and the loser knows the taker but cannot accuse him openly.
alignments.differs: The Minister takes the lady's letter for political power over her; Miles takes the governess's letter, as he says, “To see what you said about me.”

from.exact: He gave the most mournful, thoughtful little headshake. “Nothing.”

to.exact: since it is this possession, and not any employment of the letter, which bestows the power

alignments.same: What a stolen letter is worth does not lie in what it says.
alignments.differs: The Minister's power lasts only while he keeps the letter and does not use it; Miles opens the governess's letter, finds nothing in it, and has burned it.

from.exact: in which the collapse of mockery showed me how complete was the ravage of uneasiness

to.exact: I fashion the expression of my face, as accurately as possible, in accordance with the expression of his

alignments.same: The questioner wins by reading the face and mind of the one who took the letter.
alignments.differs: Dupin's reading recovers the letter without the Minister knowing; the governess forces a confession from Miles face to face, and the triumph she reads in his face ends in his death.

question: Dupin says a stolen letter's power lies in holding it, not in what it says. What power does the governess's empty letter give Miles, and what does taking it back give her?

substitution.note: Haunted and the Haunters has letters on a table taken by a ghostly hand, but no thief questioned; Jekyll burns an envelope but no one took it from him; Dracula's letters are written and sent, not stolen. Only Poe's tale has a letter taken from a table for a hold over its writer and recovered by reading the taker's mind.

claim: Both tales set a reader to judge a letter by its hand, against a man who is two things at once. Dupin sees through a disguised address because he knows the Minister as both poet and mathematician. Guest finds Hyde's hand is Jekyll's differently sloped, and Utterson, unable to think them one man, concludes that Jekyll forged for a murderer.

from.exact: the clerk laid the two sheets of paper alongside and sedulously compared their contents

to.exact: radically different from the one of which the Prefect had read us so minute a description

alignments.same: A reader sets a suspect letter against another written record and judges by the marks of the paper and hand.
alignments.differs: Dupin finds every outward mark different and concludes the letter is the same one, disguised; Guest finds the two hands nearly the same, “only differently sloped.”

from.exact: The letter was written in an odd, upright hand and signed “Edward Hyde”

to.exact: addressed, in a diminutive female hand, to D——, the minister, himself

alignments.same: A letter bears a hand chosen to mislead about whose it is.
alignments.differs: The Minister feigns a woman's hand to make the stolen letter look like his own trifling mail; Jekyll writes as Hyde to clear himself of his other self.

from.exact: “Henry Jekyll forge for a murderer!”

to.exact: You are mistaken; I know him well; he is both.

alignments.same: The inference turns on whether one man can be two kinds of man.
alignments.differs: Dupin knows the Minister is poet and mathematician at once and reasons from that; Utterson cannot think Jekyll and Hyde one man, so he reads the matching hands as forgery.

question: Utterson holds the evidence Dupin would need. What keeps him from drawing Dupin's conclusion?

substitution.note: Rue Morgue reasons from voices, not a hand; Dracula, Turn of the Screw and Haunted have letters but no one compares hands; Dorian and Usher have doubles but no letter to judge. Only Poe's tale has a disguised hand read through by knowing a man who is two things at once.

claim: Watson names Dupin and Holmes scorns him, yet Holmes works by Dupin's rules: strange details make a case easier, and a notice of a found thing brings the guilty party to the door. Dupin's notice brings the sailor, who confesses; Holmes's brings a disguised accomplice who escapes, and the police take the public credit.

from.exact: It is a mistake to confound strangeness with mystery.

to.exact: I mean for the outré character of its features

alignments.same: The detective holds that what makes a crime strange is what makes it easy to solve, while the police find it baffling.
alignments.differs: Dupin's strange details point to a killer who is not a man; Holmes's, the ring and the blood, point to a private revenge for a dead woman.

from.exact: a plain gold wedding ring, found in the roadway

to.exact: may have the animal again, upon identifying it satisfactorily

alignments.same: The detective advertises a found thing, trusting that whoever lost it will risk calling at his lodgings to claim it.
alignments.differs: Dupin's notice brings the sailor himself, who tells all; Holmes's brings the killer's friend dressed as an old woman, who takes the ring and slips out of a moving cab.

from.exact: the credit of this smart capture belongs entirely to the well-known Scotland Yard officials

to.exact: I am satisfied with having defeated him in his own castle

alignments.same: At the end the police keep the public face of the case and the private reasoner is left knowing he was right.
alignments.differs: Dupin lets the Prefect's sarcasm pass and wants nothing more; Holmes says what counts is what people are made to believe, and Watson resolves to publish the facts.

question: Holmes calls Dupin “a very inferior fellow” and then repeats his moves. What does the novel gain by naming its model and disowning it?

substitution.note: The Purloined Letter also has Dupin and a Prefect, but no advertisement and no rule that strangeness helps (there the case is hard for being too plain). The other works have no detective, no notice and no police to take the credit.

claim: Both tales set a private reasoner beside police who search with lens and measure, against a culprit who disguises a sign to mislead. Poe gives the microscope to the failing Prefect, and Dupin wins by thinking as the Minister; Doyle gives the lens to Holmes, who sees through RACHE but, thinking as the killer, is fooled by his friend.

from.exact: he whipped a tape measure and a large round magnifying glass from his pocket

to.exact: we scrutinized each individual square inch throughout the premises

alignments.same: A searcher goes over the scene inch by inch with a magnifying lens and exact measurement.
alignments.differs: In Poe it is the Prefect's routine and finds nothing; in Doyle it is the amateur's, and it gives the killer's height, cigar and nails while the police smile.

from.exact: but by a clumsy imitator who overdid his part

to.exact: so suggestive of a design to delude the beholder

alignments.same: The culprit has dressed a sign to mislead, and the reasoner sees through it because the disguise is overdone.
alignments.differs: The Minister disguises the real letter to make it look worthless; Hope writes RACHE in German style to send the police after secret societies, and the newspapers follow it.

from.exact: Now put yourself in that man’s place.

to.exact: an identification of the reasoner’s intellect with that of his opponent

alignments.same: The reasoner foresees his opponent's next move by thinking as he would think.
alignments.differs: Dupin's identification with the Minister finds the letter; Holmes rightly foresees that the killer will answer the advertisement, but not that he will send a friend in disguise.

question: Dupin outwits the Minister by thinking as he thinks; Holmes, thinking as the murderer, is tricked by a friend he never imagined. What does the detective's reasoning leave out in each tale?

substitution.note: The Rue Morgue has police and a reasoner but no minute search with a microscope and no sign disguised to deceive; Dracula, Jekyll and the haunted-house tales have no planted false lead. The rest have no search at all.

claim: Both novels end with an avenger who, getting no justice from the law, gives his life to hunting his enemy across continents and into Russia, and tells his story while dying. Victor never catches the Creature and dies with his enemy alive; Hope runs his men down in London, leaves their deaths to a choice of pills, and dies content.

from.exact: it was impossible for me to secure a conviction against them in any court

to.exact: You refuse my just demand: I have but one resource

alignments.same: The avenger finds that no court will punish his enemy and takes the punishment on himself.
alignments.differs: Victor's magistrate does not believe in the Creature; Hope's enemies' crime is twenty years old and far away, and the law has even guarded them against him.

from.exact: I have hunted you from Salt Lake City to St. Petersburg

to.exact: Amidst the wilds of Tartary and Russia, although he still evaded me, I have ever followed in his track.

alignments.same: The avenger follows his enemy across continents and into Russia, always a step behind.
alignments.differs: The Creature leaves marks to lead Victor on to the ice; Drebber and Stangerson flee to be rid of Hope, who overtakes them in London.

from.exact: I die knowing that my work in this world is done, and well done

to.exact: I feel that I shall soon die, and he, my enemy and persecutor, may still be in being.

alignments.same: Dying, the avenger tells his listeners whether his task is finished.
alignments.differs: Victor dies with his enemy alive and leaves the task to Walton; Hope has killed both men, and is found dead in his cell with a placid smile.

question: Victor calls his revenge a vice; Hope holds that he is “just as much an officer of justice” as the police. Which judgment does each novel's ending support?

substitution.note: No other earlier work on the shelf has an avenger chasing his enemy across continents after the law fails him; Dracula's hunters do pursue the Count abroad, but that novel is later (1897) and so cannot be answered by this one.

claim: Both tales fix the eye on a room whose wallpaper hangs in strips over yellow, and on marks showing who has been there. Holmes reads the bloody word, its height and the strides in the dust, and names the man. Gilman's narrator studies the paper to no conclusion and never sees that the smooch round the wall is hers.

from.exact: It is stripped off—the paper—in great patches all around the head of my bed, about as far as I can reach

to.exact: here and there great strips had become detached and hung down, exposing the yellow plaster beneath
