question: Swift's giants judge mankind from one man's boasting, Voltaire's from a mite who already despises his kind. Which satire trusts the small man's own judgment more?

substitution.note: Only Gulliver's Travels sets men against giants who measure, hold and judge them. The War of the Worlds has watchers from another planet but no giants who are measured by men or who hear them speak; Frankenstein's creature hears of wars but is not a giant among small men; the Time Machine's Eloi are small but neither measure nor are judged for their wars.

claim: Both tales set a young man above a closed garden to watch a lovely woman fed by its plants, who looks up toward him across a barrier he cannot cross and dies before him by his doing. Giovanni's cure, meant to make Beatrice ordinary, kills her; Linley lets Animula's world dry up because he cannot bear to look at it.

from.exact: unfolded a long ciliary process, with which it seized one of the gleaming fruits that glittered on its summit, and, sweeping slowly down, held it within reach of Animula.

to.exact: “Give me thy breath, my sister,” exclaimed Beatrice; “for I am faint with common air.

alignments.same: From his high window or his lens the young man watches a lovely woman in a shut garden where a plant feeds her like a sister.
alignments.differs: Beatrice's shrub is her father's making and its breath is poison; Animula's tree is no one's work, and it bends of itself to hand her fruit.

from.exact: my heart beat madly as she turned her beautiful eyes in the direction of the spot in which I stood.

to.exact: There she beheld the beautiful head of the young man

alignments.same: The woman lifts her eyes toward the place where the watching young man is hidden above her.
alignments.differs: Beatrice sees Giovanni, takes his flowers and comes to walk with him; Animula's look falls on a watcher she can never see.

from.exact: In fact, I hated to see it; for it reminded me of the natural barrier between Animula and myself.

to.exact: as poison had been life, so the powerful antidote was death

alignments.same: The woman dies before her lover's eyes because of what he did to the medium that was her life.
alignments.differs: Giovanni gives Beatrice a cure to bring her into his world, and it kills her; Linley will not look at the drop that bounds her world, and it dries away.

question: Giovanni tests Beatrice and Linley tests Animula with a lamp; neither woman is ever asked what she wants. Is Linley's love purer because Animula can never know of it, or only safer for him?

substitution.note: Only Rappaccini's Daughter has a young man watching from above a lovely woman fed by a plant in a closed garden, who looks up at him, and who dies before him of what he gives her. Georgiana in The Birth-Mark is not watched in a garden and is not cut off from her husband; Frankenstein, Moreau and the Time Machine have no such woman.

claim: Both tales give a man of science a longing for perfection his works never reach, make him find a living woman's body gross beside his ideal, and let him watch his beloved fade. Aylmer's ideal is his wife made flawless, and his draught kills her; Linley's is a creature he can never touch, and his neglect kills her.

from.exact: How I longed to discover the secret of some perfect lens

to.exact: His brightest diamonds were the merest pebbles, and felt to be so by himself, in comparison with the inestimable gems which lay hidden beyond his reach.

alignments.same: A man of science is tormented that everything he makes falls short of a perfection he can imagine but not reach.
alignments.differs: Aylmer's diamonds are a figure for his failures; Linley gets a real diamond by murder and grinds it into the perfect lens he longed for.

from.exact: Those heavy, muscular limbs, those thick ankles, those cavernous eyes, that stereotyped smile, those crudely painted cheeks!

to.exact: this slightest possible defect, which we hesitate whether to term a defect or a beauty, shocks me, as being the visible mark of earthly imperfection

alignments.same: The man looks at a woman others call beautiful and is shocked by her flesh, measured against a perfection only he sees.
alignments.differs: Aylmer is shocked by one small mark on his wife and resolves to remove it; Linley finds the most admired dancer gross all over and runs home to a creature in a drop.

from.exact: she seemed absolutely to wither away under my very eye

to.exact: Not the minutest symptom escaped him.

alignments.same: The man sits watching the woman he loves change hour by hour as she is dying.
alignments.differs: Aylmer notes each symptom in his folio and takes it for success until she speaks; Linley watches helpless and only then finds that the drop has gone.

question: Aylmer kills Georgiana by trying to perfect her; Linley kills no one he loves but loves only what he can never touch. Which tale is harder on the man of science's ideal of beauty?

substitution.note: Only The Birth-Mark has a man of science whose works fall short of hidden gems, who is shocked by a beautiful woman's flesh as imperfect, and who watches the woman he loves fade under his eye. Giovanni in Rappaccini's Daughter fears Beatrice's poison but does not find her flawed; Victor Frankenstein is shocked by his creature, not by a woman.

claim: Both tales follow a young man led into science by its dead masters, who holds human bodies cheap beside his work and, when it ends in horror, lies ill for months. Victor robs graves and recoils from the life he made; Linley kills a living man without remorse and breaks down when a being he could only watch dies.

from.exact: Neither was it at all probable that an uncultivated woman like Mrs. Vulpes should know even the name of the great father of microscopies.

to.exact: This last stroke completed the overthrow of Cornelius Agrippa, Albertus Magnus, and Paracelsus, who had so long reigned the lords of my imagination.

alignments.same: A young man's science is shaped by masters long dead, whose names rule his imagination.
alignments.differs: Victor's old masters are overthrown by modern science before he finds the secret himself; Linley calls up the founder of microscopy through a medium, and the dead man hands him the secret.

from.exact: After all, what was the life of a little peddling Jew in comparison with the interests of science?

to.exact: I collected bones from charnel houses; and disturbed, with profane fingers, the tremendous secrets of the human frame.

alignments.same: To get what his experiment needs, the young man lays hands on human bodies and puts science above them.
alignments.differs: Victor takes the dead and turns from his work with loathing; Linley kills a living man for his diamond and reasons coolly that science gives him the right.

from.exact: I crawled feebly to my bed, from which I did not rise for many months.

to.exact: This was the commencement of a nervous fever, which confined me for several months.

alignments.same: When his work ends in horror the young man falls senseless and lies ill for months.
alignments.differs: Victor is struck down by the life he gave and is nursed back by Clerval; Linley by the death he could not stop, and rises a pauper laughed at as the mad microscopist.

question: Victor feels the guilt of the graves he robbed but not at first of the being he made; Linley feels nothing for Simon and everything for Animula. What does each man's grief show about what he valued?

substitution.note: Only Frankenstein has a young man shaped by dead masters of science, who takes human bodies for his work and who falls into months of illness when it ends in horror. Aylmer in The Birth-Mark takes no bodies and does not fall ill; Griffin in The Invisible Man and Moreau do not collapse; Jekyll dies rather than lying ill.

claim: Abbott's 'lilliputian' Lineland plays Swift's game of scale: a visitor meets a tiny king who takes his realm for the world, comes from a people who make a woman a parallelogram, and at home measures his household by what he saw. Swift's worlds differ in size; Abbott's differ in dimension, and cannot be shown.

from.exact: was persuaded that the Straight Line which he called his Kingdom, and in which he passed his existence, constituted the whole of the world, and indeed the whole of Space

to.exact: most mighty Emperor of Lilliput, delight and terror of the universe, whose dominions extend five thousand blustrugs (about twelve miles in circumference) to the extremities of the globe

alignments.same: A visitor far bigger than the natives meets a tiny king who takes his little realm for the whole world.
alignments.differs: Golbasto boasts a twelve-mile empire while he fights Blefuscu next door; the Monarch of Lineland cannot conceive that anything lies outside his line.

from.exact: a Woman, though popularly called a Straight Line, is, really and scientifically, a very thin Parallelogram

to.exact: If they would, for example, praise the beauty of a woman, or any other animal, they describe it by rhombs, circles, parallelograms, ellipses, and other geometrical terms

alignments.same: A people who think only in lines and figures speak of a woman as a geometrical figure, down to the parallelogram.
alignments.differs: The Laputans praise a woman's beauty in figures; in Flatland a woman is a figure, the meanest, and the Square's science only grants her some breadth.

from.exact: because I could not compare what I saw in Two Dimensions with what it really was if seen in Three, and could hardly refrain from making my comparisons aloud

to.exact: I looked down upon the servants, and one or two friends who were in the house, as if they had been pigmies and I a giant.

alignments.same: Home again, the traveller keeps measuring his own household by the scale of the world he has left.
alignments.differs: Gulliver's family thinks he has lost his wits until the habit wears off; the Square's comparisons spoken aloud bring him to prison while the vision itself fades.

question: Swift's traveller is an outsider among kings and geometers; Abbott's Square is himself a geometer of the land he mocks. Does that turn Flatland's satire on its narrator more than Gulliver's?

substitution.note: Only Gulliver's Travels has a tiny king claiming the world before a giant visitor, a people who describe women in geometrical figures, and a traveller who comes home measuring his household by another scale. Micromégas has giants and mites but no king, no women made figures, and no return home; The Time Machine's Traveller comes home but measures nothing by scale.

claim: Both books pair a guide from a larger world with a lesser companion: the guide corrects him for calling a strange shape irregular, talk turns to beings more perfect still, and they meet a speck sure the universe is its own. Voltaire's Sirian feels those higher beings himself; Abbott's Sphere denies them until his pupil argues.

from.exact: methinks I see no Solid, but a Plane such as we infer in Flatland; only of an Irregularity which betokens some monstrous criminal

to.exact: Everything appears irregular to you here, you say, because everything on Saturn and Jupiter is drawn in straight lines.

alignments.same: A traveller from a straight-lined world calls a strange form irregular and offensive, and his guide from a larger world puts it down to habit.
alignments.differs: The Saturnian dwarf thinks no one of sense could live on the jagged Earth; the Square takes the Cube for a monstrous criminal, since in Flatland irregularity is crime.

from.exact: so doubtless there is One above you who combines many Spheres in One Supreme Existence

to.exact: and yet we still have a kind of vague feeling, a sort of worry, that warns us that there are even more perfect beings

alignments.same: Talk between the higher visitor and the lesser one turns to beings more perfect than the higher.
alignments.differs: Micromégas feels them himself and tells the Saturnian so; the Square must press them on the Sphere, who answers that a Fourth Dimension is inconceivable.

from.exact: He is himself his own World, his own Universe; of any other than himself he can form no conception

to.exact: He argued that their people, their worlds, their suns, their stars, had all been made uniquely for mankind.

alignments.same: Travellers from greater worlds look down on the tiniest creature they meet and hear it claim the universe for itself.
alignments.differs: Voltaire's giants laugh at the Thomist and leave the mites a book of blank pages; the Square scolds the Point, which takes his rebuke for its own thought.

question: Micromégas admits there are beings above him; the Sphere calls a Fourth Dimension inconceivable. Is Abbott's satire aimed at the teacher as much as at the Point, and is the Square's craving for more any different from the Point's content?

substitution.note: Only Micromégas pairs a guide from a larger world with a companion from a smaller one who finds a world irregular for want of straight lines, and has a tiny creature claim the universe before them. Gulliver's Travels has no guide and companion; The War of the Worlds' Martians neither speak of higher beings nor meet a talking speck; The Time Machine has no guide.

claim: Both books argue from flat figures to solids for a dimension their hearers cannot see, show a higher being only in sections, and tell creatures bound to two directions that only their own limits bar the next. Wells names the fourth dimension Time and builds a machine for it; Abbott's Square never rises by his own will.

from.exact: You know how on a flat surface, which has only two dimensions, we can represent a figure of a three-dimensional solid, and similarly they think that by models of three dimensions they could represent one of four

to.exact: And does it not now follow that, in this region, when I see a Plane and infer a Solid, I really see a Fourth unrecognized Dimension

alignments.same: A reasoner argues from flat figures and solids, by analogy, that there must be a fourth dimension no one can see.
alignments.differs: The Time Traveller leans on mathematicians' models and makes the fourth Time; the Square reasons from his own lifting into Space toward a fourth direction of space.

from.exact: All these are evidently sections, as it were, Three-Dimensional representations of his Four-Dimensioned being, which is a fixed and unalterable thing.

to.exact: your country of Two Dimensions is not spacious enough to represent me, a being of Three, but can only exhibit a slice or section of me, which is what you call a Circle

alignments.same: A being of more dimensions appears in the lower world only as a section of itself.
alignments.differs: Wells's sections are portraits of one man at eight, fifteen and seventeen; Abbott's are circles that shrink and grow as the Sphere rises and sinks.

from.exact: I admit we move freely in two dimensions. But how about up and down? Gravitation limits us there.

to.exact: You could leave the Plane yourself, if you could but summon up the necessary volition.

alignments.same: Creatures who move freely in two directions are told that only a limit of their own keeps them from the next.
alignments.differs: The Traveller says a civilised man beats gravity in a balloon and may beat time with a machine; the Square never rises by his own will and is carried up and flung down.

question: Wells's guests doubt the Traveller until he vanishes; the Square cannot vanish for anyone in Flatland. What changes when a fourth dimension can be travelled and not only argued for?

substitution.note: Only Flatland argues for an unseen dimension from flat figures and solids and shows a higher being in sections. Micromégas and Gulliver's Travels play with size, not dimension; The Machine Stops speaks of a lost sense of space but not of a fourth dimension or of sections; The Invisible Man's unseen body is a matter of optics.

claim: Both tales tell of a man who learns his people know less space than there is, reaches a world above, is condemned by rulers who forbid such worlds, and ends hoping for rebels outside. Forster's Kuno climbs up with his own arms and has met those rebels; Abbott's Square is carried up and has no convert.

from.exact: We say 'space is annihilated,' but we have annihilated not space, but the sense thereof.

to.exact: Exactly: you see you do not even know what Space is. You think it is of Two Dimensions only

alignments.same: A man is told that his people do not know what space is, and that a whole part of it is missing from their sense of it.
alignments.differs: Kuno says it himself, of a sense men once had and he won back by walking; the Sphere tells the Square of a dimension Flatland never knew.

from.exact: It was just what the Committee thought, when they threatened me with Homelessness.

to.exact: enjoining the arrest, imprisonment, or execution of any one who should pervert the minds of people by delusions, and by professing to have received revelations from another World

alignments.same: The rulers threaten death or prison to whoever claims a world beyond the one they allow.
alignments.differs: Kuno's Committee punishes a way out found without the Machine's leave; Flatland's Council punishes talk of revelation while its President keeps the Sphere's visits in secret archives.

from.exact: They are hiding in the mist and the ferns until our civilisation stops.

to.exact: may stir up a race of rebels who shall refuse to be confined to limited Dimensionality

alignments.same: The condemned man ends his story pinning his hope on rebels outside the world that shut him in.
alignments.differs: Kuno has seen and loved the people of the surface and dies as the Machine stops; the Square, without a convert, hopes only that his memoirs reach some dimension.

question: Kuno's mother calls him mad; the Square's brother saw the Sphere himself and still disbelieves. Why does each author leave the visionary's story with a relative who will not believe it?

substitution.note: Only Flatland joins a world above that its people lack the sense to know, a council that condemns those who claim it, and a closing hope for rebels. The Time Machine's Traveller is doubted but never condemned; Gulliver's Travels has no rulers who forbid other worlds; The Diamond Lens's world below is watched, not entered or forbidden.

claim: Both tales send a man who sees more among people without his sight: they have no word for what he sees, he takes sight for a title to rule, and his boast turns the whole people on him. Abbott's Square dreams it and wakes; Wells's Nunez cannot strike, recants, and keeps his eyes by climbing out.

from.exact: There is no such word as see

to.exact: though I know not what you mean by ‘right’ and ‘left.’ But I deny that you saw these things.

alignments.same: Told what the visitor sees, the natives deny he saw it and treat his word for it as empty.
alignments.differs: The blind man rules the word 'see' out of the language; the Monarch keeps 'right' and 'left' but takes them for Northward and Southward and says the Square heard and dreamed.

from.exact: They little know they've been insulting their heaven-sent king and master.

to.exact: Behold, I am become as a God.

alignments.same: The one who sees more than those about him decides his sight makes him their lord.
alignments.differs: Nunez plans to rule the blind and ends their serf; the Sphere answers the Square at once that seeing everything would not make a cut-throat a God.

from.exact: You are blind, and I can see. Leave me alone!

to.exact: Hearing these words the King advanced towards me with a menacing cry as if to pierce me through the diagonal

alignments.same: Crying out that he sees what they cannot, the visitor has the whole people closing in to strike him.
alignments.differs: Nunez strikes once, flees over the valley wall and comes back starving to recant; the Square stands spell-bound and wakes to his breakfast bell.

question: Nunez's sight is real and useless among the blind; the Square's sight of Lineland is real and convinces no one. Do the two tales mock the visitor's pride, or the people who will not believe him, or both?

substitution.note: Only Flatland has a visitor with a sense the natives lack and no word for, who boasts of it as superiority and is set upon by the whole people. The Invisible Man's Griffin means to rule by his advantage and is hunted, but no one lacks a word for it; Gulliver's Travels and Micromégas play with size, not a missing sense; The Machine Stops' Kuno claims no rule.

claim: Both tales bring a visitor to a people so long sheltered from danger that they have changed; in the dark they handle him with soft hands, and he stands armed against them. The Traveller longs to kill Morlocks; Nunez cannot strike a blind man, and the sightless prove the able ones.

from.exact: But life was very easy in that snow-rimmed basin, lost to all the world, with neither thorns nor briars, with no evil insects nor any beasts save the gentle breed of llamas

to.exact: For countless years I judged there had been no danger of war or solitary violence, no danger from wild beasts, no wasting disease to require strength of constitution, no need of toil.

alignments.same: A people cut off for generations from danger, wild beasts and hard toil have lost a power their forebears had.
alignments.differs: The Eloi's ease sinks them into languor and decay; the valley people lose only their eyes and stay strong and able, ordering their world to their needs.

from.exact: touching him with soft, sensitive hands, smelling at him, and listening at every word he spoke

to.exact: I was roused by a soft hand touching my face.

alignments.same: People who live without light examine the newcomer with soft hands.
alignments.differs: The Morlocks flee the Traveller's struck match and later drag at him; the blind crowd round Nunez, hold him and lead him to their elders to be taught.

from.exact: it was impossible for him to hit a blind man in cold blood

to.exact: And I longed very much to kill a Morlock or so.

alignments.same: Holding a tool turned weapon among people of the dark, the visitor weighs striking them down.
alignments.differs: The Traveller with his iron mace feels no humanity in the Morlocks and wants to kill; Nunez with his spade finds he cannot hit a blind man in cold blood.

question: The Traveller reads the dark-dwellers as a warning about his own society; Nunez's blind are kindly, ordered and right by their own lights. Why does Wells give the people of the dark the better of the visitor the second time?

substitution.note: Only The Time Machine has a people changed by long security, a visitor touched by soft hands in the dark, and a visitor who stands armed against the dark-dwellers and thinks of killing. The Machine Stops has security and atrophy but no soft hands in the dark and no armed visitor; Gulliver's Travels has small people crawling over a bound man but no darkness or changed race; The Lost World's ape-men are fought but were never sheltered.

claim: Both books set a traveller proud of his country before hosts who question him closely and take notes, and make him dodge the answers that would shame it. Swift's giant king sums up his people as odious vermin; Gilman's women pass no sentence, and Van comes to be less proud of his world.

from.exact: I had always been proud of my country, of course. Everyone is.

to.exact: that might have enabled me to celebrate the praise of my own dear native country in a style equal to its merits and felicity.

alignments.same: Before the questioning starts, the traveller is sure his country is as good as any and means to show it off.
alignments.differs: Van states his pride flatly as what everyone feels; Gulliver wishes for the tongue of Demosthenes to praise England, a boast Swift turns to irony from the first.

from.exact: They listened closely, with the usual note-taking.

to.exact: frequently taking notes of what I spoke, as well as memorandums of what questions he intended to ask me.

alignments.same: The hosts write down the traveller's account of his country and come back to it with sharper questions.
alignments.differs: The king works alone through six audiences toward a verdict; the women question as a body, compare the answers and build an outline of the outer world.

from.exact: I am ashamed to say that I equivocated.

to.exact: I artfully eluded many of his questions, and gave to every point a more favourable turn, by many degrees, than the strictness of truth would allow.

alignments.same: Pressed on his country's faults, the traveller owns that he dodged the questions to spare its name.
alignments.differs: Gulliver calls his evasion a laudable partiality and blames the king's seclusion; Van is ashamed of it, having hidden infanticide behind a few 'perverts, or crazy' women.

question: Swift's king judges and Gulliver blames the judge; Gilman's women never judge and Van judges himself. Which way of questioning a visitor makes the sharper satire on his country?

substitution.note: Only Gulliver's Travels has a traveller praise his country to hosts who take notes and press him, and who evades them out of partiality. The Country of the Blind's Nunez explains the great world to elders who disbelieve him, but hides nothing; Micromégas, Flatland and The Time Machine have no host questioning a visitor about his country's faults.

claim: Both books bring a man of science to a land without struggle, bred like a garden to human use, where the old marks of sex are gone, and set him theorising that only struggle makes strength. Wells's frail Eloi bear the theory out; Gilman's strong mothers ask whether struggle is the only law.

from.exact: By the most prolonged and careful selection and exclusion they had developed a race of cats that did not sing!

to.exact: In the end, wisely and carefully we shall readjust the balance of animal and vegetable life to suit our human needs.

alignments.same: The visitor finds plants and beasts bred over long ages to suit human needs, the whole land made a garden.
alignments.differs: Wells's breeders are long gone and their garden runs to waste over a fading race; Gilman's women are still at work, breeding cats and replanting forests for food.

from.exact: were strikingly deficient in what we call “femininity.”

to.exact: In costume, and in all the differences of texture and bearing that now mark off the sexes from each other, these people of the future were alike.

alignments.same: The visitor notices that the people lack the marks of sex his own world takes for nature.
alignments.differs: The Traveller reads it as family and fierce maternity fading with need; Van finds motherhood the centre of everything and decides 'feminine charms' were only grown to please men.

from.exact: I explained that the laws of nature require a struggle for existence, and that in the struggle the fittest survive, and the unfit perish.

to.exact: Strength is the outcome of need; security sets a premium on feebleness.

alignments.same: The visitor accounts for the land by a law that strength comes only from struggle and need.
alignments.differs: The Eloi's frail limbs bear the Traveller out; women grown 'not by competition, but by united action' ask Van whether these laws of nature are all the laws he has.

question: Wells and Gilman both imagine a people freed from war, beasts and want. Why does one find them sinking into childishness and the other find them stronger and wiser than the visitor?

substitution.note: Only The Time Machine has a visitor theorise that a land bred like a garden and freed from struggle has lost the marks of sex and must breed feebleness. Gulliver's Houyhnhnms teach both sexes alike but Gulliver draws no law of struggle; The Machine Stops and The Country of the Blind have sheltered peoples but no lost marks of sex and no visitor's theory of struggle.

claim: Both tales seal a people in a mountain valley when an upheaval closes the only way out; a visitor arrives sure his one advantage makes him their king, and his try at force is overpowered. Nunez flees and recants; Terry is bound, tried and sent home, his manhood no title to rule.

from.exact: there occurred a volcanic outburst, with some local tremors, and the result was the complete filling up of the pass—their only outlet.

to.exact: one whole side of the old Arauca crest slipped and came down in thunder, and cut off the Country of the Blind for ever from the exploring feet of men

alignments.same: A volcanic upheaval brings a mountainside down on the only way out, and a small people live sealed in their valley for generations.
alignments.differs: Wells's valley keeps its men and loses its sight to a disease; Gilman's loses its men to war and the quake, and its women learn to bear daughters alone.

from.exact: I’ll get myself elected king in no time—whew!

to.exact: the fifth found the King of the Blind still incognito, as a clumsy and useless stranger among his subjects.

alignments.same: The visitor takes for granted that his one advantage over the people will make him their king.
alignments.differs: Terry counts on manhood among women and boasts before he lands; Nunez trusts his eyes among the blind and is a clumsy stranger before he can proclaim himself.

from.exact: Terry dashed about like a madman; he would cheerfully have killed them—he told me that, himself—but he couldn’t.

to.exact: He thought chiefly of ways of fighting and conquering these people, and it grew clear that for him no practicable way was possible.

alignments.same: Having tried force, the visitor longs to fight and conquer the people but finds he cannot.
alignments.differs: Terry is caught, bound and put under anaesthetic by stronger women, then tried; Nunez strikes one man with his spade and flees, beaten by numbers and his horror of hitting the blind.

question: Nunez must give up his eyes to marry Medina-saroté; Terry must give up mastering to keep Alima. What does each valley ask the visitor to give up, and is it the same thing?

substitution.note: Only The Country of the Blind seals a people in a mountain valley by a slide that closes the way out, and brings a visitor who expects to be king by his one advantage and cannot conquer by force. Gulliver is held by small and great peoples but never sealed in a valley or sure of a crown; The Invisible Man's Griffin plans a reign of terror in an open village; Flatland's Square only dreams his kingship.

claim: Both tales carry a man out of his own time and back: he reads his river valley anew, must make out a new rule, and tells a tale his hearers half doubt. Rip sleeps twenty years and shrugs off a revolution; the Traveller rides to 802,701, theorizes, and offers his tale as lie or prophecy.

from.exact: but the Thames had shifted, perhaps, a mile from its present position

to.exact: There stood the Kaatskill mountains—there ran the silver Hudson at a distance—there was every hill and dale precisely as it had always been

alignments.same: Come into another age, the man takes his bearings from the river valley he knew.
alignments.differs: Rip's Hudson and hills are just as they were and only the village is strange; for the Traveller even the Thames has moved and nothing of his London is left.

from.exact: Communism,’ said I to myself.

to.exact: Rip, in fact, was no politician; the changes of states and empires made but little impression on him

alignments.same: Each man has to make out what new order of rule has grown up while he was gone.
alignments.differs: The Traveller names the future's politics on his first evening and theorizes on it; Rip slept through a revolution, cares nothing for it, and is glad only that his wife's rule is over.

from.exact: Take it as a lie—or a prophecy. Say I dreamed it in the workshop.

to.exact: Some always pretended to doubt the reality of it, and insisted that Rip had been out of his head

alignments.same: Home again, the man tells what befell him, and his hearers may take it for a dream or a delusion.
alignments.differs: Rip's neighbours split, and the old Dutch believe him; the Traveller himself offers his friends the choice of lie or dream, and the Editor calls him a storyteller.

question: Rip loses twenty years and gains an idle old age; the Traveller loses a few hours and brings back the end of mankind. In which tale does the lost time cost more?

substitution.note: Only The Time Machine takes a man into another age and back, sets him reading a changed river valley, has him guess its government, and lets him offer his tale as a dream. Gulliver's Travels and the other voyages cross space, not time; The War of the Worlds' narrator comes home after days, under the same rule. Flatland's Square, Herland's visitors and the Country of the Blind's Nunez reach other worlds in space, not another age, and none comes home to a river valley that has changed.

claim: Both tales picture a man who outlives his time: dated by the king he remembers, lost in the new talk, rid of his wife. Swift's struldbrugs never die, are despised, and lose wife and estate by law; Rip loses twenty years in a night, is revered as a patriarch, and counts his wife's death a deliverance.

from.exact: a loyal subject of the King, God bless him!

to.exact: the usual way of computing how old they are, is by asking them what kings or great persons they can remember

alignments.same: A man left over from an earlier age is known by the king he still names as his own.
alignments.differs: The struldbrugs are dated coolly against the history of reigns; Rip's loyalty to King George in the new republic gets him hooted as a tory and a spy.

from.exact: which were a perfect Babylonish jargon to the bewildered Van Winkle

to.exact: the struldbrugs of one age do not understand those of another

alignments.same: The talk of the living has moved on, and the old man cannot follow it.
alignments.differs: Swift's immortals stay foreigners in their own country for ever; Rip in time gets back into the regular track of village gossip.

from.exact: he had got his neck out of the yoke of matrimony

to.exact: should not have their misery doubled by the load of a wife

alignments.same: Outliving his time frees the old man from his wife, and marriage is called a yoke or a load.
alignments.differs: Swift's law dissolves the marriage as a cold mercy inside a misery that never ends; Dame Van Winkle dies of her own temper, and Rip's release is the tale's happy ending.

question: Swift makes outliving one's age a curse and Irving makes it a holiday. What has Rip that the struldbrugs lack?

substitution.note: Only Gulliver's Travels has old men left over from their age who are dated by the kings they remember, cannot understand the new tongue, and are released from a wife. The Time Machine's Traveller cannot follow the Eloi either, but he has no king to betray him and no wife to lose. Flatland, Herland and The Country of the Blind have no old man dated by his king or freed from a wife.

claim: Both tales frame a Hudson legend alike: a traveller's view of a drowsy Dutch village, a tale retold by mouth, an end that splits doubters from old Dutch believers. Rip's tale settles into the narrator's own version, backed by a historian's heir; Sleepy Hollow's teller owns he believes half of it.

from.exact: In the bosom of one of those spacious coves which indent the eastern shore of the Hudson

to.exact: Whoever has made a voyage up the Hudson must remember the Kaatskill mountains.

alignments.same: Each tale opens as a traveller's view from the Hudson of a sleepy village of the old Dutch settlers, before any person of the story appears.
alignments.differs: Rip's village is seen from a passing boat and the Revolution will change it; Sleepy Hollow is a still nook the narrator thinks keeps the same trees and families.

from.exact: The old country wives, however, who are the best judges of these matters, maintain to this day that Ichabod was spirited away by supernatural means

to.exact: The old Dutch inhabitants, however, almost universally gave it full credit.

alignments.same: The tale closes by splitting its hearers: some doubt, and the oldest Dutch folk hold the marvel true to this day.
alignments.differs: Rip's doubters only call him flighty, and a historian's heir confirms the haunted mountains; in Sleepy Hollow the pumpkin and Brom's laugh hand the reader the doubters' case.

from.exact: “Faith, sir,” replied the story-teller, “as to that matter, I don’t believe one-half of it myself.”

to.exact: It at last settled down precisely to the tale I have related

alignments.same: Each tale is a story told over by mouth before it is written, and its last words turn to the teller.
alignments.differs: Rip's tale, after varying, settles into the narrator's version, which he stands behind; Sleepy Hollow is a shabby storyteller's piece, defended by a mock syllogism and half disowned.

question: Irving lets an old historian's heir vouch for Rip and lets Sleepy Hollow's teller disbelieve half his tale. Why does the second legend need a teller who doubts it?

substitution.note: Only Rip Van Winkle opens on a Dutch village seen from the Hudson, ends by splitting doubters from old Dutch believers, and turns at the close to the man who told it. The Turn of the Screw and The Haunted and the Haunters frame a ghost story with a teller, but neither has the village legend or the split verdict. Recheck: The Country of the Blind and Herland also open on a hidden community found by an outsider, but neither has a Hudson Dutch village, a tale retold by mouth, or a verdict split between doubters and old believers.

claim: Both tales set a sham spectre with a hollow vegetable for a head against a haunting: Brom's pumpkin, the twins' turnip. Irving's prank routs a Yankee who believes Cotton Mather, and the valley goes on believing; Wilde's routs a real ghost among Americans who believe in none, and the hoax is signed.

from.exact: But there is no such thing, sir, as a ghost, and I guess the laws of Nature are not going to be suspended for the British aristocracy.

to.exact: was a perfect master of Cotton Mather’s “History of New England Witchcraft,” in which, by the way, he most firmly and potently believed.

alignments.same: An American comes into an old haunted place with a settled creed about spirits.
alignments.differs: Ichabod, the Connecticut schoolmaster, believes every word of Mather and dreads every sound; the American Minister believes in no ghosts and treats the haunting as a stain for detergent.

from.exact: and he found himself clasping a white dimity bed-curtain, with a sweeping-brush, a kitchen cleaver, and a hollow turnip lying at his feet!

to.exact: was found the hat of the unfortunate Ichabod, and close beside it a shattered pumpkin.

alignments.same: After the night's terror, the spectre's head is found on the ground by morning light, and it is a hollowed vegetable.
alignments.differs: Irving's searchers find the pumpkin and still decide the Hessian took Ichabod; Wilde's ghost holds the turnip in his own arms and is left no doubt of the hoax.

from.exact: He had been tricked, foiled, and out-witted!

to.exact: always burst into a hearty laugh at the mention of the pumpkin

alignments.same: Rough young pranksters play ghost against one who stands in their way, and the prank wins.
alignments.differs: Brom never owns his prank, only laughs, and wins the heiress; the twins sign theirs on a placard, and the ghost they fool swears vengeance and fails.

question: Irving's prank never confesses itself and Wilde's comes with a placard. In which tale is the ghost more real, and whom does each joke serve?

substitution.note: Only The Canterville Ghost has pranksters raise a sham spectre whose head is a hollow vegetable, set against an American's fixed creed about ghosts. The Hound of the Baskervilles has a schemer's painted hound but no vegetable head and no believer routed by a joke; Northanger Abbey has a credulous reader but no sham spectre. Recheck: The Country of the Blind and Herland set an outsider's creed against a closed people, but have no haunting, no prankster and no sham spectre.

claim: Both tales test a man's reading against a haunting known for a headless ghost, and both hint at a living hand behind it. Ichabod cons Cotton Mather till dusk and flees what may be his rival in disguise; Bulwer's narrator carries Macaulay as an antidote, hunts the ghost, and finds a will far stranger than a prank.

from.exact: you remember in Germany how disappointed we were at not finding a ghost in that old castle, which was said to be haunted by a headless apparition?

to.exact: is the apparition of a figure on horseback, without a head.

alignments.same: The place's fame rests on a headless apparition the hero has heard tell of.
alignments.differs: Ichabod dreads the Hessian and meets him on the road; Bulwer's narrator went looking for a headless ghost in Germany and was sorry to find none.

from.exact: there was so much of healthfulness in the style, and practical life in the subjects, that it would serve as an antidote against the influences of superstitious fancy.

to.exact: there con over old Mather’s direful tales, until the gathering dusk of evening made the printed page a mere mist before his eyes.

alignments.same: The man's chosen book goes with him toward the haunted dark and shapes how he meets it.
alignments.differs: Ichabod reads witch-lore till dusk and walks home in terror of every sound; Bulwer's narrator packs Macaulay's Essays against fancy and keeps his eye on their daylight sense.

from.exact: must originate in some human being gifted by constitution with the power so to present them, and having some motive so to do

to.exact: which led some to suspect that he knew more about the matter than he chose to tell.

alignments.same: Behind the haunting may stand a living person with a motive, not a spirit.
alignments.differs: Bulwer's narrator reasons his way to a hidden will of uncanny power and finds it; Irving gives only a hint that a jealous rival was the horseman, and the old wives deny it.

question: Bulwer's sceptic explains his haunting and is more afraid than before; Irving's believer is frightened by what may be a joke. Which tale makes the supernatural harder to dismiss?

substitution.note: Only The Haunted and the Haunters names a headless apparition, sends its man in with a chosen book against fancy, and traces the haunting to a living agent with a motive. The Canterville Ghost has sceptics but no book and no headless ghost; The Hound of the Baskervilles has a human agent and a read legend, but its spectre is a hound and Holmes carries no antidote. Recheck: The Country of the Blind and Herland test a man's beliefs in a strange place, but have no headless ghost, no chosen book against fancy, and no living hand behind a haunting.

claim: Both tales send a lone man by night through haunted woods, where a dark fellow-traveller keeps pace and a church tune sounds, and both doubt it was real. Irving's horseman is likely a rival's prank and costs Ichabod a courtship; Hawthorne's meeting may be a dream, yet it blights Brown's trust in everyone for life.

from.exact: He arose at Goodman Brown’s approach and walked onward side by side with him.

to.exact: On mounting a rising ground, which brought the figure of his fellow-traveller in relief against the sky, gigantic in height, and muffled in a cloak, Ichabod was horror-struck on perceiving that he was headless!

alignments.same: On the night road a dark stranger rises by the wayside and keeps pace with the lone traveller, his fellow-traveller.
alignments.differs: Ichabod's companion is silent and he flees it in terror; Brown's came by appointment, looks like his own kin, and talks him onward.

from.exact: He knew the tune; it was a familiar one in the choir of the village meeting-house.

to.exact: shutting his eyes, broke forth with involuntary fervor into a psalm tune.

alignments.same: In the haunted dark a church tune is heard, the music of the village meeting on Sundays.
alignments.differs: Ichabod, the singing-master, sings a psalm as a charm against the goblin; Brown hears the meeting-house hymn sung by the devil's own congregation.

from.exact: Had Goodman Brown fallen asleep in the forest and only dreamed a wild dream of a witch-meeting?

to.exact: The old country wives, however, who are the best judges of these matters, maintain to this day that Ichabod was spirited away by supernatural means

alignments.same: The tale leaves open whether the night's marvel was real and lets the reader take an earthly explanation.
alignments.differs: Irving's choice, goblin or prank, is fireside talk; Hawthorne waves the question aside, since dream or not, Brown lives distrustful and dies in gloom.

question: Ichabod's psalm fails against a goblin who may be Brom Bones; Brown's hymn is sung by the witches themselves. What does each tale make of a man who carries his church into the woods?

substitution.note: False for every other tale: none has both a fellow-traveller keeping pace on a night road and a church tune in the haunted dark. Nearest: Rip Van Winkle (stranger leads Rip up the mountain, but no hymn, no fear of a spirit, no doubt left open by the narrator); Haunted and the Haunters (no road, no companion). Country of the Blind and Herland (added in the corrected ordering): no night road, no fellow-traveller, no church tune.

claim: Both tales show a young husband taught by a night vision that a stain of sin marks every human being, his wife too, and the knowledge parts them. Brown's devil shows the whole earth one blood spot and Brown shrinks from Faith for life; Aylmer sees it in one crimson mark and kills Georgiana erasing it.

from.exact: selecting it as the symbol of his wife’s liability to sin, sorrow, decay, and death

to.exact: and shall exult to behold the whole earth one stain of guilt, one mighty blood spot.

alignments.same: A blood-red stain stands for the sin and mortality every human shares, the husband's wife among them.
alignments.differs: The devil spreads the stain over the whole earth and every heart; Aylmer gathers it into one small hand on Georgiana's cheek, small enough to cut away.

from.exact: Truth often finds its way to the mind close muffled in robes of sleep

to.exact: it was a dream of evil omen for young Goodman Brown

alignments.same: A dream shows the husband what he thinks of his wife, and he cannot unknow it by day.
alignments.differs: Aylmer's dream of the knife tells a truth about himself, which he then acts out; Brown's dream claims to show others' sins, and he never asks whether it lied.

from.exact: With the morning twilight Aylmer opened his eyes upon his wife’s face and recognized the symbol of imperfection

to.exact: Often, waking suddenly at midnight, he shrank from the bosom of Faith

alignments.same: Waking beside his wife, the husband sees the mark of sin in her and recoils.
alignments.differs: Brown's recoil lasts a long marriage with children and ends in a gloomy grave; Aylmer's turns into an experiment that perfects Georgiana and kills her.

question: Brown cannot stop seeing sin in Faith; Aylmer cannot stop seeing it on Georgiana's cheek. Which husband sees truly, and which tale blames the seeing?

substitution.note: False for every other tale: no other husband sees a stain of sin shared by all in his own wife. Nearest: Rappaccini's Daughter (Beatrice tainted, but Giovanni is a suitor, no dream, no universal stain); Yellow Wallpaper (husband and night, but he sees no sin in her). Country of the Blind and Herland (added in the corrected ordering): Nunez's bride's people would take his eyes, not see sin in her; Herland has no husband's night vision.

claim: Both tales set a young man and the woman he loves before a dark father, who welcomes the pair into a nature set apart, with a font turned to evil. Brown cries to Faith to resist and doubts her all his life; Giovanni curses Beatrice as poison, and dying she asks whether the poison was his.

from.exact: thou art no longer lonely in the world. Pluck one of those precious gems from thy sister shrub and bid thy bridegroom wear it in his bosom.

to.exact: said the dark figure, “to the communion of your race.

alignments.same: A dark father figure presents the young man and woman to each other as a pair joined in a new, fallen nature.
alignments.differs: The devil welcomes them into the sin common to all mankind; Rappaccini boasts that his poison has set them apart from common men and women.

from.exact: Let us to church and dip our fingers in the holy water at the portal!

to.exact: Herein did the shape of evil dip his hand and prepare to lay the mark of baptism upon their foreheads

alignments.same: A hand dipped in a font would mark the pair with a baptism that seals evil instead of washing it away.
alignments.differs: Hawthorne's font is a rock basin of water, blood or flame at the devil's altar; Giovanni only mocks, picturing their poisoned fingers fouling a church's holy water.

from.exact: Oh, was there not, from the first, more poison in thy nature than in mine?

to.exact: But Goodman Brown looked sternly and sadly into her face, and passed on without a greeting.

alignments.same: After the night's revelation the young man turns from the woman he loved, believing her tainted.
alignments.differs: Faith may be innocent and Brown never asks her; Beatrice speaks last, dies of his cure, and turns the charge back on Giovanni's own suspicious nature.

question: Brown and Giovanni each learn that the woman they love is tainted, and each turns cold. Is the poison in Faith and Beatrice, or in the men who look at them?

substitution.note: False for every other tale: none sets a lovers' pair before a dark father who welcomes them into a fallen nature by a font. Nearest: Birth-Mark (husband, not a father, and no rite); Frankenstein (a maker, but no pair is welcomed); Dracula (a dark host, but no pair, no font). Country of the Blind and Herland (added in the corrected ordering): Yacob gives his daughter on condition of the blinding, but no font and no evil nature; Herland has no dark father.

claim: Both tales bring a Puritan village to see that every face hides a sin, and the knowledge parts a man from the woman pledged to him. Brown learns it from the devil and shrinks from Faith and his minister; Hooper wears it as a veil, so his betrothed and his people shrink from him.

from.exact: I look around me, and, lo! on every visage a Black Veil!

to.exact: shall exult to behold the whole earth one stain of guilt, one mighty blood spot.

alignments.same: The tale's last great speech tells its hearers that no one is clean: every human face hides a sin.
alignments.differs: The devil says it at a witch-meeting to win Brown to despair; the dying Hooper says it to rebuke those who shunned him, his own veil included.

from.exact: The subject had reference to secret sin, and those sad mysteries which we hide from our nearest and dearest

to.exact: When the minister spoke from the pulpit with power and fervid eloquence

alignments.same: A Sunday sermon in the village meeting-house turns, for its hearers, on the sins that pious people hide.
alignments.differs: Brown, in the pew, takes the preacher for a gray blasphemer; Hooper's hearers feel the veiled preacher has found out their own hoarded iniquity.

from.exact: Lift the veil but once, and look me in the face

to.exact: Often, waking suddenly at midnight, he shrank from the bosom of Faith

alignments.same: The sign of hidden sin comes between the man and the woman who loves him.
alignments.differs: Brown pulls away from his wife Faith, who stays beside him; Hooper begs Elizabeth to stay, she will not wed him veiled, yet she nurses him at his death.

question: Brown is shown other people's secret sins and trusts no one again; Hooper shows none and makes everyone think of their own. Which tale lays the hidden sin on the one who sees it?

substitution.note: False for every other tale: none has a sermon on hidden sin heard by a Puritan congregation, a speech that every face hides guilt, and a man parted from his beloved by it. Nearest: The Birth-Mark (a stain of sin on one face, not every face; no sermon); Rappaccini's Daughter (poison, not sin hidden by the pious); Jekyll and Hyde (one man's hidden self, no congregation).

claim: Both tales set a sign of sin and sorrow on a face that the beloved asks to have taken away and its bearer dreads in the mirror. Hooper chose his veil, keeps it and is buried in it; Georgiana's birthmark means sin only to Aylmer, whose cure kills her as it fades.

from.exact: selecting it as the symbol of his wife’s liability to sin, sorrow, decay, and death

to.exact: an ambiguity of sin or sorrow, which enveloped the poor minister

alignments.same: A mark on a face is read as a symbol of sin or sorrow, and it darkens how others see its bearer.
alignments.differs: Hooper puts the veil on himself and keeps its meaning hidden; Aylmer chooses the meaning for a mark his wife was born with.

from.exact: Cannot you remove this little, little mark, which I cover with the tips of two small fingers?

to.exact: First lay aside your black veil: then tell me why you put it on.

alignments.same: The woman bound to the man asks that the mark on the face be taken away, so that love can go on.
alignments.differs: Elizabeth asks Hooper to lift his own veil and he refuses; Georgiana asks her husband to remove her mark, and he does, at the cost of her life.

from.exact: whenever she dared to look into the mirror, there she beheld herself pale as a white rose and with the crimson birthmark stamped upon her cheek.

to.exact: catching a glimpse of his figure in the looking-glass, the black veil involved his own spirit in the horror with which it overwhelmed all others.

alignments.same: Seeing the marked face in a mirror, its bearer feels the horror the mark stirs in others.
alignments.differs: Hooper flees and after avoids every mirror but keeps the veil; Georgiana learned the horror from her husband's gaze and yields herself to his cure.

question: Hooper refuses to lift his veil and dies with it; Aylmer removes the birthmark and his wife dies with it gone. What does each tale say about a sign of sin that someone tries to take off?

substitution.note: False for every other tale: none has a mark on a face read as sin or sorrow that a loved one begs to have removed and that its bearer sees in a mirror. Nearest: Young Goodman Brown (stain of guilt over the earth, no mark on a face, no mirror); Dorian Gray (sin shown on a hidden portrait, not on the face, and no one asks him to remove it); Rappaccini's Daughter (poison in the body, not a sign on the face).

claim: Both books end with a maimed or bereaved man swearing to hunt a creature over far seas, and a ship's company begging to turn home. Walton gives way, and Victor's quarry writes to lead him on; Ahab holds his course against Starbuck, after a whale whose malice he cannot know is there.

from.exact: and I’ll chase him round Good Hope, and round the Horn, and round the Norway Maelstrom, and round perdition’s flames before I give him up.

to.exact: I swear to pursue the dæmon, who caused this misery, until he or I shall perish in mortal conflict.

alignments.same: A man the creature has wounded swears aloud to pursue it to the ends of the earth until one of them dies.
alignments.differs: Victor swears alone at night by his family's graves; Ahab swears on the quarter-deck and makes the crew drink and swear with him, so the hunt becomes theirs.

from.exact: But Ahab’s glance was averted; like a blighted fruit tree he shook, and cast his last, cindered apple to the soil.

to.exact: The die is cast; I have consented to return, if we are not destroyed.

alignments.same: Far out at sea, the captain is begged to turn the ship for home, for the sake of the men and the families waiting for them.
alignments.differs: Walton, whose quest is not a vendetta, consents and turns south though Victor scorns it; Ahab, whose quest it is, turns his eyes from Starbuck's and keeps on.

from.exact: That inscrutable thing is chiefly what I hate; and be the white whale agent, or be the white whale principal, I will wreak that hate upon him.

to.exact: Follow me; I seek the everlasting ices of the north, where you will feel the misery of cold and frost, to which I am impassive.

alignments.same: The pursuer believes the fleeing creature wills the chase and means him harm.
alignments.differs: Victor's creature cuts words in trees and stone to lead him north, so its will is plain; Ahab has only a dumb whale and hates it for a malice he cannot prove.

question: Walton turns back and lives to write; Ahab will not, and only Ishmael survives to tell. Does Moby-Dick make Walton's choice look like cowardice, as Victor said, or like the only sane end?

substitution.note: Only Frankenstein has an oath of pursuit sworn by a man the creature has wronged, a ship's company begging its captain to turn home, and a fleeing creature that leaves messages for its pursuer. Twenty Thousand Leagues has a crew that wants to turn back and a captain who asks three days, but Farragut has no wrong to avenge and his monster leaves no word; Dracula's hunters swear an oath, but no ship's crew pleads to turn home.

claim: Verne names Moby Dick among the papers' monsters, then stages a whale-hunt in its manner: a captain's money for the first sighting, a crew that wants home, a famous harpooner. Ahab can only suspect a will behind the whale he strikes; Verne's monster is a ship, and the man inside asks why he was harpooned.

from.exact: Besides, Captain Farragut had spoken of a certain sum of two thousand dollars, set apart for whoever should first sight the monster, were he cabin-boy, common seaman, or officer.

to.exact: look ye, whosoever of ye raises me that same white whale, he shall have this gold ounce, my boys!

alignments.same: The captain promises money to whichever man aboard first sights the one sea-beast the ship is hunting.
alignments.differs: Farragut's prize is a sum spoken of that the watchers reckon in dollars; Ahab hammers a gold coin to the mainmast before the crew as the seal of his own vendetta.

from.exact: Captain Farragut (as Columbus did) asked for three days’ patience.

to.exact: But Ahab’s glance was averted; like a blighted fruit tree he shook, and cast his last, cindered apple to the soil.

alignments.same: After a long hunt the men want to go home, and the captain must answer them.
alignments.differs: Farragut bargains for three days and promises to turn the wheel for Europe; Ahab looks away from Starbuck's plea and holds his course.

from.exact: Was it unintentionally that Mr. Ned Land struck me with his harpoon?

to.exact: That inscrutable thing is chiefly what I hate; and be the white whale agent, or be the white whale principal, I will wreak that hate upon him.

alignments.same: The hunters ask whether a will stands behind the sea-beast they have struck.
alignments.differs: Ahab cannot know whether the whale is agent or principal and strikes anyway; in Verne the harpooned beast is a steel ship, and its master answers in the first person.

question: Verne turns Melville's unknowable whale into a machine with a man inside who can explain himself. Is Nemo the answer to Ahab's question, or does a monster that talks lose what made the white whale terrible?

substitution.note: No other graph work has a ship hunting one sea-beast with a reward for the first sighting, a crew that wants to turn home, and a harpooner; Frankenstein shares only the plea to turn back, and its creature is no sea-beast.

claim: Both books let a calm reasoner weigh a despised people as stock: their young are to be thinned by a practice borrowed from husbandry, their skins tanned for shoes, and sound reforms set aside as hopeless. Swift's Houyhnhnms judge brutes and spare their lives; his projector judges his own countrymen and kills a hundred thousand a year.

from.exact: the number of people will be thereby much lessened in the kingdom. This I freely own, and was indeed one principal design in offering it to the world

to.exact: would in an age put an end to the whole species, without destroying life

alignments.same: A speaker offers the public a scheme for the young of a despised people, taken from the breeding of beasts, whose aim is that there be fewer of them.
alignments.differs: The Houyhnhnm's expedient is gelding, which leaves the Yahoos alive and ends them over an age; the projector's is butchery at one year old, and he owns the shrinking as his design.

from.exact: the skin of which, artificially dressed, will make admirable gloves for ladies, and summer boots for fine gentlemen

to.exact: I supplied it with the skins of Yahoos dried in the sun

alignments.same: Skins of human-shaped creatures are cured and made into footwear.
alignments.differs: Gulliver soles his own shoes with the hides of brutes he has learned to loathe; the projector sells the skins of Irish children as boots for fine gentlemen.

from.exact: Of teaching landlords to have at least one degree of mercy towards their tenants

to.exact: with many other wild, impossible chimeras, that never entered before into the heart of man to conceive

alignments.same: Plain reforms, rulers serving the public good or landlords showing mercy, are listed only to be dismissed as beyond hope.
alignments.differs: Gulliver calls the Lagado professors who urge them mad; the projector names them as the true remedies and builds his own scheme out of despair that anyone will try them.

question: The Houyhnhnms are horses judging brutes, the projector an Irishman judging Irishmen: does Swift's satire cut deeper when the reasoner is one of his victims' own kind?

claim: Both books reason calmly to men who eat men: one class, ground down by rent, ends as fatted stock bred for another's table. Swift's rich are to eat the children of the poor, in a scheme never carried out; Wells's descendants of the workers eat the descendants of the rich, and the Traveller's calm breaks over Weena.

from.exact: These Eloi were mere fatted cattle, which the ant-like Morlocks preserved and preyed upon—probably saw to the breeding of.

to.exact: twenty thousand may be reserved for breed, whereof only one fourth part to be males; which is more than we allow to sheep, black cattle, or swine

alignments.same: People are kept like cattle, fattened and bred so that others may eat them.
alignments.differs: Swift's breeders are the Irish poor selling their young to landlords; Wells's cattle are the heirs of the rich, kept by the workers' heirs below.

from.exact: Once they were there, they would no doubt have to pay rent, and not a little of it, for the ventilation of their caverns; and if they refused, they would starve or be suffocated for arrears.

to.exact: very proper for landlords, who, as they have already devoured most of the parents, seem to have the best title to the children

alignments.same: Rent paid to the rich decides whether the poor live or starve.
alignments.differs: Swift's landlords devour the poor in figure and are offered their children in fact; Wells's rent kills the rebellious workers and breeds survivors who will one day eat their landlords' heirs.

from.exact: I tried to look at the thing in a scientific spirit.

to.exact: they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected

alignments.same: A reasoner looks coolly at human beings dying or eaten and finds no cause to be troubled.
alignments.differs: The projector never wavers; the Traveller's coolness lasts a few sentences, until he sees Weena dancing at his side.

question: Swift's cannibals are the landlords and Wells's are the workers' children: which reversal makes the reader more uneasy about his own class?

claim: Both travellers reach a sealed land of reason where the stones men kill for are dirt and no one disputes an opinion, and both leave it. Gulliver is sent away in tears and comes home loathing his kind; Candide asks to go, to be richer than kings, loading his sheep with the scorned pebbles.

from.exact: who have an inconceivable passion for the pebbles and dirt of our land, for the sake of which they would murder us to the last man

to.exact: there are certain shining stones of several colours, whereof the Yahoos are violently fond

alignments.same: A sage of the land of reason speaks of coloured stones that the brutes outside crave and fight over.
alignments.differs: The Houyhnhnm tells of Yahoos digging in his fields, leaving Gulliver to see Europe in them; the El Dorado elder names the Europeans outright, and his roads are paved with the stones.

from.exact: here we are all of one opinion, and we know not what you mean by monks

to.exact: I could bring my master to understand the meaning of the word opinion, or how a point could be disputable

alignments.same: The people of the land of reason cannot conceive the quarrels over opinion that Europe lives by.
alignments.differs: Gulliver's master lacks the very idea, since reason leaves nothing in doubt; the elder holds one faith with everyone and cannot conceive monks who burn those of another.

from.exact: If we abide here we shall only be upon a footing with the rest

to.exact: I took leave of my master and lady and the whole family, my eyes flowing with tears, and my heart quite sunk with grief

alignments.same: The traveller leaves the best country he has found, in a craft its people help him make.
alignments.differs: Gulliver is exhorted out by the assembly and weeps at going; Candide asks leave, so as to be richer than kings at home, and the King calls him foolish.

question: Gulliver would have stayed among the Houyhnhnms for ever; Candide leaves El Dorado after a month. Which satire is harder on the traveller, and which on the land of reason?

substitution.note: Only Gulliver's Travels has a sealed country of reason whose people scorn the stones men fight for, cannot grasp disputes of opinion, and see the traveller off. Herland is sealed and unmoved by Terry's necklace but has quarrels of opinion and no scorned stones; The Country of the Blind is sealed and Nunez flees it, but its people are not a commonwealth of reason; Micromégas and Flatland have no such land. Swapping Candide for Rip Van Winkle or the Time Machine leaves no land that is left by choice for gold.

claim: Both tales set a doctor proving all was made for man against armies of men killing each other, and end with man's purpose asked of a higher wisdom and left unanswered. Micromégas looks down from the stars and laughs; Candide suffers below, and a dervish says a sultan ignores the mice on his ship.

from.exact: Observe, that the nose has been formed to bear spectacles—thus we have spectacles.

to.exact: He argued that their people, their worlds, their suns, their stars, had all been made uniquely for mankind.

alignments.same: A doctor of the schools proves that the things around men were made on purpose for them.
alignments.differs: The Thomist claims the stars for man before two giants from the stars, who laugh; Pangloss proves noses were made for spectacles to a pupil who believes every word.

from.exact: A million regimented assassins, from one extremity of Europe to the other, get their bread by disciplined depredation and murder, for want of more honest employment.

to.exact: there are 100,000 madmen of our species wearing hats, killing 100,000 other animals wearing turbans, or being massacred by them

alignments.same: A philosopher tells of his own kind's armies, counted by the hundred thousand, killing one another across the earth.
alignments.differs: The mite says they die for a heap of mud owned by a sultan they never saw; Martin says they kill for bread, proof that a malignant being rules the globe.

from.exact: When his highness sends a ship to Egypt, does he trouble his head whether the mice on board are at their ease or not?

to.exact: when the ancient secretary opened it, he saw nothing but blank pages

alignments.same: Men who ask a higher wisdom what they are for are given no answer.
alignments.differs: The Sirian promises a book showing the point of everything and leaves it blank; the Dervish refuses outright, likening men to mice in a sultan's ship, and Candide turns to his garden.

question: Micromégas sees men as atoms from a giant's height, Candide's dervish as mice from a sultan's. Does the joke change when a man on earth, not a visitor from the stars, says men do not matter?

substitution.note: Only Micromégas has a learned man claiming all things were made for man, a count of the hundred thousands killed in war, and a promised answer that proves empty. Gulliver's Travels has the war verdict but no doctor of final causes and no withheld answer; in Flatland the Sphere refuses the Square's talk of higher dimensions, but there is no doctor of design and no war count; A Modest Proposal reckons people but asks nothing of a higher wisdom.

claim: Both books take at its word the saying that the rich devour the poor: a respectable man advises eating people so the meat lasts, a child is sold for the parents' gain, and the eater sits at a European table. Swift only proposes it; in Candide it has been done, and the eaten tell it.

from.exact: exhorting them not to kill us all at once

to.exact: twenty thousand may be reserved for breed, whereof only one fourth part to be males

alignments.same: A man of standing advises those who would eat human flesh to keep part of the stock alive so that the meat lasts.
alignments.differs: Swift's projector plans a market for peacetime Ireland; the Iman preaches to starving Janissaries under siege, and the women live on with one buttock each.

from.exact: thou hast the honour of being the slave of our lords, the whites, which is making the fortune of thy father and mother

to.exact: besides the gain of eight shillings sterling per annum by the sale of their children

alignments.same: The sale of a poor child is promised to bring the parents gain.
alignments.differs: The projector counts the breeders' profit in shillings; the slave's mother sold him with a blessing, and he says the sale has made no one's fortune, least of all his.

from.exact: This is the price at which you eat sugar in Europe.

to.exact: very proper for landlords, who, as they have already devoured most of the parents, seem to have the best title to the children

alignments.same: The comfortable are said to eat the bodies of the poor who work for them.
alignments.differs: Swift's landlords devouring their tenants is a figure turned into a proposal; the slave's hand and leg, cut off at the sugar mill, are what the European's sugar really costs.

question: Swift's victims never speak; Voltaire's old woman and the slave of Surinam tell what was done to them. Which way of telling leaves the reader more implicated?

substitution.note: Only A Modest Proposal reckons the eating of the poor as an economy: stock reserved for breed, children sold for shillings, landlords as eaters. The Time Machine has Morlocks eating Eloi but no one advising it, no sale of children and no European table; Gulliver's Travels tans Yahoo skins but eats no one; Moby-Dick's cannibals are not the poor eaten by the rich.

claim: A poor man of the pen walks home alone at midnight from a richer man's feast, is set upon in a lonely waste, and leaves a bundle of effects and a ghost in the town's talk. Irving's goblin was a living rival and Ichabod prospers elsewhere; Gogol's clerk dies, and his ghost robs the great.

from.exact: The huge, melancholy expanse looked to him like a sea.

to.exact: Far below him the Tappan Zee spread its dusky and indistinct waste of waters

alignments.same: Going home alone after midnight from a party at a richer house, the man sees the empty land open before him like dark water.
alignments.differs: Ichabod rides home already crestfallen, refused by the heiress; Akaki walks home cheered by champagne and his new cloak, and his dread comes only at the square, before the robbers.

from.exact: left nothing behind him but a bundle of goose-quills, a notebook of white paper, three pairs of socks, some trouser buttons, and his old coat

to.exact: examined the bundle which contained all his worldly effects

alignments.same: When the man is gone, his goods are counted out: a bundle of stockings and old clothes and the tools of his trade.
alignments.differs: Ichabod has only vanished, his goods are searched and his verses burned; Akaki is dead, nothing is even sealed, and the narrator never asks who took his things.

from.exact: there appeared every night a spectre in a uniform like that of the chancellery officials

to.exact: was reported to be haunted by the ghost of the unfortunate pedagogue

alignments.same: After the man is gone, rumour makes him a ghost that walks the places of his old life.
alignments.differs: Irving's ghost only chants a psalm tune, and a farmer reports Ichabod alive; Gogol's dead clerk comes back with his fists and strips the cloak off the man who scolded him.

question: Irving lets a rival dressed as a goblin drive Ichabod out of the valley into a career; Gogol lets the dead clerk come back as a robber of cloaks. Which ending gives the poor scribe more?

substitution.note: Only Sleepy Hollow has the poor man of the pen going home alone at midnight from a richer man's feast, an inventory of his bundle when he is gone, and a ghost of him in the town's talk. Canterville Ghost and The Haunted and the Haunters have ghosts but no victim made into one; Rip Van Winkle comes home alive and is not inventoried; Young Goodman Brown walks at night but from no feast and is not robbed. No other story in the graph has a clerk robbed on his way home.

claim: A man of the pen serves superiors who rule his wording, and rank shows him the door. Werther, who loves to transpose, is eased out of a noble assembly by a kind count and smarts at the gossip; Akaki, who can only copy, is shouted out of a great man's room and dies.

from.exact: altering the headings of various documents, and here and there changing the first personal pronoun into the third

to.exact: he has a deadly antipathy to all those transpositions of which I am so fond

alignments.same: An office paper is judged word by word, and a change in its wording sets the clerk apart from his superior.
alignments.differs: Werther wants to transpose and a pedant forbids it; Akaki is asked by a kind director to change a pronoun, sweats over it and begs to be given something to copy.

from.exact: with whom you are speaking? Do you consider before whom you are standing?

to.exact: I perceive the company is rather displeased at your being here.

alignments.same: Before onlookers, a man of rank tells a subordinate he has come where his rank does not admit him.
alignments.differs: The count speaks kindly at a window and Werther bows out smiling; the Superintendent shouts to impress a friend, and Akaki has to be dragged out half conscious.

from.exact: In his whole life he had never been so scolded by a superior official

to.exact: the minister gave me a reprimand,—a gentle one it is true, but still a reprimand

alignments.same: A reprimand from above falls on the subordinate and stays with him.
alignments.differs: Werther's minister softens his with a generous letter and Werther is at peace for a week; Akaki's scolding sends him out into the storm, and he dies of the fever.

question: Werther leaves the assembly and drives off to read Homer at sunset; Akaki goes out into the storm. What does Gogol's clerk lack that lets Goethe's hero turn an insult into a sorrow?

substitution.note: Only Werther has a subordinate whose papers a superior rules word by word, a reprimand from a minister and a scene where a man of rank shows him out of company. Northanger Abbey turns Catherine out of a great house, but she is no clerk and no one judges her wording; Gulliver's Travels has courts and ministers but no copying subordinate. No other story in the graph has an office clerk.
